### 5.60. The holomorphic incidence class and shrinking normal supports

Let \(M\) be a complex manifold of dimension \(m\ge1\), and let
\(S\subset M\) be a smooth hypersurface. Locally choose coordinates
\((z,f)\), where \(z\in\mathbb C^{m-1}\) and \(S=\{f=0\}\).
A holomorphic coefficient line \(F\) has degree zero.
We construct the single-pole class in the actual microlocal Hom
complex, retaining its real phase and connecting sign. We also
identify an actual finite differential-operator module that
injects into every nonzero conormal stalk.

The proof uses the injective and relative-support constructions
of [§5.34, R.5–R.7](#5-34-full-current-resolutions-and-controlled-proper-image-comparison); the connecting and ordered coefficient
conventions of [§5.35, V.1–V.6](#5-35-relative-cones-unshifted-cup-and-the-normalized-trace); the strict cofinal cones of
[§5.45, IG.1](#5-45-the-full-geometric-infinite-order-kernel-ring-and-its-canonical-product); the finite real-stalk witnesses of [§5.53,
RM.3–RM.9](#5-53-real-kernel-comparison-for-all-constant-euler-matrices); and the projection and open/closed comparisons of
[§5.59, OCM.A–OCM.B](#5-59-open-and-closed-incidence-in-the-actual-microlocal-hom-complex). Every further comparison is proved below.
The construction does not assert a finite-\(E\) simple-generator
theorem or either normalized inverse kernel product.

#### HI.0. The support functor and its polar sign

Use the microlocal Hom support model OCM.4. On \(M\times M\)
write the second point as
\((z',f')=(z+\zeta,f+n_f)\).
On the closed subset \(f'=0\),

\[
 \zeta=z'-z,\qquad n_f=-f.
 \tag{HI.1}
\]

For a nonzero conormal covector with normal coefficient \(p\),
define the degree-full hypersurface support complex

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathfrak h_{f,p}(K)
   =\mathop{\rm colim}_{U,H}R\Gamma_H(U;K),\\
 C_S(H)\setminus0
   \subset\{\Re(fp)>0\}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.2}
\]

The arrows are actual restrictions and support enlargements.
The positive polar sign in HI.2 is forced by HI.1:
the diagonal condition is \(-\Re(n_fp)>0\).
If \(\mathfrak m_{S,p}\) denotes the negative-polar support
complex, then

\[
 \mathfrak h_{f,p}=\mathfrak m_{S,-p}.
 \tag{HI.3}
\]

Thus the antipodal operation is explicit; \(p\) and \(-p\)
are not identified. All comparisons below use HI.2.
For a bounded coefficient complex they are comparisons in
every degree, not only its top cohomology.

#### HI.1. Continuous homotopies with pulled-back coefficients

We need a coefficient-preserving comparison that does not
differentiate a continuous radius function. Suppose
\(a:Z\to B\), \(E=a^{-1}K\), and
\(h:Z\times[0,1]\to Z\) is continuous with
\(a h=a\operatorname{pr}_Z\). Then

\[
 h^{-1}E=\operatorname{pr}_Z^{-1}E.
 \tag{HI.4}
\]

The endpoint pullbacks induce the same map on derived sections,
with finite cochain homotopies in the models used here.
Here is the comparison explicitly.

Extend \(h\) continuously to an open interval \(J\) containing
\([0,1]\), constantly beyond the two endpoints. The ordinary
projection \(Z\times J\to Z\), with coefficient \(E\), has
the inverse-image unit

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 R\Gamma(Z;E)\\
 \longrightarrow
 R\Gamma(Z\times J;\operatorname{pr}_Z^{-1}E).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.5}
\]

This is a quasi-isomorphism. OCM.8–OCM.9 proves it using a
real de Rham resolution tensored over \(\mathbb C\) with
the coefficient sheaf and a smooth contraction of \(J\).
The local integral uses finitely many coefficient expressions
along a compact interval, so arbitrary sheaves are allowed.
Both endpoint restrictions are inverse to HI.5 and therefore
agree in the derived category.

There is a pullback on derived sections for the continuous map
\(h\). To construct it, pull back an injective resolution
term by term, then apply the germ-product injective resolution
R.12–R.13 to the pulled-back terms. Its augmentation and total
differential give the pullback map. In each fixed total degree,
only finitely many columns occur, because the original complex
is bounded below. The finite comparison procedure R.6 compares
the two endpoint maps with the smooth interval model.
The interval integration operator there supplies their
degree-minus-one homotopy. Pullback of the smooth scalar
forms by the continuous map \(h\) is never used.

Consequently a homotopy equivalence over \(B\) induces a
quasi-isomorphism on derived sections of \(a^{-1}K\).
The same statement applies after every base restriction.
For any finite diagram, the comparisons and homotopies have
finitely many entries in the degrees in use; intersect their
finitely many domains to obtain a common actual witness.

#### HI.2. A shrinking ball family and its zero-radius comparison

Let \(B\) be a coordinate manifold, \(H\subset B\) closed,
and let \(\rho:B\to[0,R/2)\) be continuous and zero off \(H\).
On \(X=B\times B_R^k\), with projection \(\pi\), put

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 G_0=H\times\{0\},\\
 G_\rho=\{(u,v):u\in H,\\
 |v|\le\rho(u)\}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.6}
\]

Both supports are closed. Their projections to \(B\) are
proper: over a compact base subset, the fibre coordinates
lie in the closed ball of radius strictly less than \(R/2\),
and the support is closed in that compact product.

For \(k>0\), set \(r=|v|\). On \(X\setminus G_0\) define
the base-preserving map

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 Q(u,v)=\left(u,\frac{\psi_{\rho(u)}(r)}r\,v\right),\\
 r>0,\\
 \psi_\rho(r)=\rho+(1-\rho/R)r.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.7}
\]

At \(v=0\), which is in this domain only for \(u\notin H\),
define \(Q(u,0)=(u,0)\). It is continuous there:
outside the closed set \(H\), \(\rho\) is zero on a
neighbourhood, so this map is the identity.
Everywhere else continuity follows from \(r>0\) and continuity
of \(\rho\).

For \(0<r<R\) the new radius is strictly between \(\rho\)
and \(R\). Thus \(Q\) maps \(X\setminus G_0\) to
\(X\setminus G_\rho\). It is a homeomorphism with inverse
given, for \(r>\rho\), by the radial function

\[
 \psi_\rho^{-1}(r)
   =\frac{R(r-\rho)}{R-\rho}.
 \tag{HI.8}
\]

The inclusion \(j:X\setminus G_\rho\hookrightarrow
X\setminus G_0\) is homotopy inverse to \(Q\).
Both homotopies use the same radial formula

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 r_s=r+s\rho(1-r/R),\\
 0\le s\le1.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.9}
\]

On the first complement it stays positive; on the second it
stays greater than \(\rho\). It stays below \(R\) in either
case, and is the identity at \(v=0\) off \(H\).
All maps keep \(u\) fixed. HI.1 therefore shows that the
restriction map on complement complexes is a quasi-isomorphism
for every coefficient \(\pi^{-1}K\).

Use the same whole-domain complex on the two supports in
the relative convention OCM.2. The inclusion \(G_0\subset
G_\rho\) gives a map of the two relative complexes, equal
to the identity on the whole-domain entry and to restriction
on the complement entry. Its cone is acyclic, since the
complement map is a quasi-isomorphism. This proves

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 R\pi_*R\Gamma_{G_0}(\pi^{-1}K)\\
 \longrightarrow
 R\pi_*R\Gamma_{G_\rho}(\pi^{-1}K)\\
 \hbox{is a quasi-isomorphism.}
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.10}
\]

The pushforward is essential in this sheaf assertion:
the argument holds over every base open, and the map is the
canonical support enlargement. Its quasi-inverse is constructed
from the complement maps and their two homotopies through
the relative cones. No shrinking-fibre base-change formula
is assumed. When \(k=0\), the two supports coincide and
HI.10 is the identity.

#### HI.3. The zero-normal orientation class

We give the complete normalization for the zero-radius support.
In one real coordinate \(v\), the punctured interval has
negative and positive components. Contract each interval
component, and the full interval, using OCM.9.
The resulting finite relative complex is

\[
 \mathbb C
 \xrightarrow{\ d\ }\mathbb C^2,
 \qquad d(a)=(a,a),
 \tag{HI.11}
\]

in degrees zero and one. Order the complement entries as
negative, positive. The positive connecting class of the
step function \(1_{\{v>0\}}\), in convention V.1, is
\((0,-1)\). Define

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \epsilon(b_-,b_+)=b_--b_+,\\
 \iota(c)=(0,-c),\\
 h(b_-,b_+)=b_-.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.12}
\]

Then \(\epsilon\iota=1\), and direct substitution gives
\(dh+hd=1-\iota\epsilon\). The connecting class has
\(\epsilon(0,-1)=1\). This fixes its sign, rather than
choosing a sign after a trace calculation.

For \(k\) ordered real normal coordinates, use the finite
coordinate-puncture cube and tensor HI.11–HI.12 in that
order. The complement cube comparison is V.6 and R.7.
All its intersections are products of intervals and
signed interval components; the coefficient contraction
HI.5 applies on each intersection. The alternating
finite cube therefore computes the actual relative
complex, including each complement entry.

For homogeneous tensor factors \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\), its
contracting homotopy is

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 H(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_k)\\
 =\sum_{i=1}^k(-1)^{\sum_{j<i}|x_j|}\\
 {}\cdot P x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes P x_{i-1}\\
 {}\otimes h x_i\\
 {}\otimes x_{i+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_k,\\
 P=\iota\epsilon.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.13}
\]

The tensor differential differentiates the \(i\)-th factor
with sign \((-1)^{\sum_{j<i}|x_j|}\).
The identity \(dh+hd=1-P\) telescopes to

\[
 dH+Hd=1-P^{\otimes k}.
 \tag{HI.14}
\]

The surviving tensor has degree \(k\) and normal trace one.
Put these normal factors before the coefficient complex
\(K\). Its differential on the surviving factor is
\((-1)^k d_K\); thus its target is \(K[-k]\).
The terms involving \(d_K\) cancel in HI.14 because \(H\)
lowers normal degree by one. A permutation of the real
normal coordinates multiplies the orientation class by
the sign of that permutation, since the one-coordinate
classes have odd degree.

This constructs, naturally on base opens,

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 R\Gamma_{B\times\{0\}}(\pi^{-1}K)\\
 \simeq i_*K[-k].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.15}
\]

where \(i(u)=(u,0)\). Outside the zero section the left side
vanishes. Along that section the finite cube just computed
gives exactly the right side; its augmentations and trace
give the displayed maps. The finite tensor homotopy gives
both inverse identities. For \(k=0\), the empty normal
tensor is one in degree zero.

#### HI.4. The supported Thom comparison, including the collapsed fibre

For two closed supports \(A,B\), the support functors commute
in the derived category:

\[
 R\Gamma_A R\Gamma_B
   =R\Gamma_{A\cap B}.
 \tag{HI.16}
\]

Here is the injective justification in the present coefficient
category. For an injective sheaf \(I\),
\(\Gamma_B I=\mathcal Hom(\mathbb C_B,I)\), by applying
Hom to the exact open/closed sequence OCM.18. This is
injective, since its left-adjoint tensor over \(\mathbb C\)
is exact. Hence an injective resolution can compute both
successive support functors. On its terms, requiring both
supports is exactly requiring their intersection. This
proves HI.16.

Apply HI.16 to \(H\times B_R^k\) and \(B\times\{0\}\).
Together with HI.15 and exact closed direct image, it gives

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 R\Gamma_{G_0}(\pi^{-1}K)\\
 \simeq i_*R\Gamma_H(K)[-k].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.17}
\]

The support enlargement HI.10 is therefore the desired
comparison for the full shrinking family. On these supports
ordinary and proper pushforward agree: in the injective
support model each term is supported on the proper closed
set \(G_\rho\) or \(G_0\). Over a compact base subset the
normal support is compact inside the fixed larger ball.
Thus its support remains proper before any trace is applied.
Since \(\pi i=1\), HI.17 proves the normalized formula

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 R\pi_*R\Gamma_{G_\rho}(\pi^{-1}K)\\
 \simeq R\Gamma_H(K)[-k].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.18}
\]

**Theorem HI.A.** HI.18 holds for every closed \(H\), every
continuous \(\rho\) zero off \(H\) with \(0\le\rho<R/2\),
and every bounded complex \(K\) of complex-vector sheaves.
It includes \(\rho=0\), every boundary point of \(H\), and
every collapsing fibre. The normal orientation is the
ordered class of trace one in HI.12–HI.15.

**Proof.** HI.7–HI.10 compares the actual relative complexes,
and HI.11–HI.17 computes the zero-radius complex with
its tensor signs. Properness was checked on the entire
closed support, not inferred from individual fibres.
These maps are natural in \(K\). Their homotopies and
resolution comparisons have finitely many entries in
each degree, so a finite family of equalities is realized
after one actual common restriction. \(\square\)

This proof also gives compatibility with support enlargement
and base restriction. Any two comparison choices induce
the inverse of the same canonical support-enlargement
map HI.10, with the same trace-one normal class.
The two radial homotopies and the finite tensor homotopy
supply the corresponding finite equality witnesses.
It does not replace a boundary stalk by cohomology of
one isolated fibre.

#### HI.5. A hypersurface in the doubled support model

Let \(F\) be any bounded coefficient complex on \(M\).
On \(M\times M\), Hom from the closed second hypersurface
is the corresponding supported complex:

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 R\mathcal Hom(q_2^{-1}\mathbb C_S,q_1^!F)\\
 =
 R\Gamma_{\{f'=0\}}(q_1^{-1}F)[2m].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.19}
\]

Indeed \(q_2^{-1}\mathbb C_S\) is the constant sheaf on
the closed subset \(f'=0\), extended by closed direct
image. The injective argument of HI.16 identifies its
Hom with sections supported there. The projection
normalization is OCM.16. These observations prove HI.19
on the actual injective complexes.

Its coefficient is constant in the second \(f'\)-normal
variable. HI.15 in its two real coordinates therefore
identifies HI.19 with the closed direct image from \(f'=0\)
of that coefficient shifted by \([2m-2]\).
The normal orientation is the positive complex orientation,
with trace one.

Now apply the diagonal support functor OCM.3. Intersecting
its supports with \(f'=0\) is justified by HI.16.
In coordinates HI.1, choose the cofinal round cone

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 a=\Re(e^{i\theta}f),\\
 b=\Im(e^{i\theta}f),\\
 a\ge0,\quad b^2+|\zeta|^2\le L^2a^2.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.20}
\]

Its nonzero vectors have strict diagonal polar margin
at least \(1/\sqrt{1+L^2}\). Choose the margin and a
nearby-covector neighbourhood before the support domains.
IG.1's compact unit-cone argument makes these cones
cofinal; the change \(n_f=-f\) gives exactly the sign
in HI.2.

The projected support and the tangent-ball radius are

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 H_\theta=\{a\ge0,\ |b|\le La\},\\
 \rho(f)\\
 =\sqrt{\max\{L^2a_+^2-b^2,0\}},\\
 a_+=\max(a,0).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.21}
\]

This radius is continuous and zero off \(H_\theta\).
It vanishes on the sector boundary, including \(f=0\).
After choosing the tangent-normal domain \(B_R^{2m-2}\),
shrink the actual \(f\)-disc so that \(L|f|<R/2\).
Then the entire closed tangent support has a common
inner/outer collar. HI.A applies with \(k=2m-2\).
When \(m=1\), there is no tangent normal and its comparison
is the \(k=0\) identity.

The first normal shift \([-2]\), the tangent-normal
shift \([-(2m-2)]\), and the projection shift \([2m]\)
cancel:

\[
 2m-2-(2m-2)=0.
 \tag{HI.22}
\]

This cancellation records the degrees of the maps just
constructed; it is not used as a substitute for those maps.
The ordered first normal block has real dimension two.
Moving it past the remaining real block gives sign
\((-1)^{2(2m-2)}=1\). The change \(f\mapsto-f\) also
preserves real orientation, since its real determinant
is positive. It changes the polar sign as in HI.1–HI.3,
not the trace-one orientation class. The coefficient
line \(F\) remains ungraded throughout.

**Theorem HI.B.** On the nonzero conormal to \(S\),
there is the natural, sign-specified comparison

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbb C_S,F)_p\\
 \simeq\mathfrak h_{f,p}(F),\\
 \mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbb C_S[-1],F)_p\\
 \simeq\mathfrak h_{f,p}(F)[1].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.23}
\]

**Proof.** HI.19 reduces the second normal direction by
HI.15. On each cofinal round support the tangent-normal
comparison is HI.18. Restrictions and support maps commute
with these comparisons, by the support-enlargement
compatibility of HI.A. Their filtered colimit is HI.23.
The shift in the second line is contravariance in the
first argument, with the same convention as OCM.22.
Every finite diagram has the actual common collars,
resolutions and cochain witnesses specified above.
\(\square\)

These local comparisons agree after an ordinary coordinate
change straightening the hypersurface. The supports are
transported by the derivative on the compact normal cone,
with a strict smaller polar margin, as in [BCT.1](#5-56-whole-real-kernel-coordinate-transport-and-balanced-comparison).
The relative restriction maps are literal pullbacks on
the two opens; HI.15 uses the induced real orientation.
Two straightening charts have the same orientation class
and the same canonical support-enlargement comparison,
so HI.A's homotopies give equality on an overlap after
one common refinement. Holomorphic coefficient frame
changes are coefficient maps and commute with these
constructions.

#### HI.6. Off-conormal vanishing

For completeness the doubled construction introduces no
extra characteristic directions. Outside \(S\), a small
enough diagonal neighbourhood misses \(f'=0\), so HI.19
has zero microlocal stalk. At a covector with nonzero
tangent component, choose a tangent vector \(e_\zeta\)
with positive polar pairing, small enough to lie in the
chosen tangent ball.

Enlarge the round cone so that \((-e_\zeta,0)\) lies in
its strict interior. This is possible: that vector has
strictly positive negative-polar pairing. Increasing the
finite aperture preserves a positive margin and contains
the finitely many earlier supports. Shrink the \(f\)-disc
so that \((-e_\zeta,f)\) is still in that interior and
\((e_\zeta,-f)\) remains outside the cone.

For fixed \((z,f)\), contract the tangent variable to
\(e_\zeta\). In the full normal vector this is

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 (\zeta,-f)\longmapsto\\
 (1-s)(\zeta,-f)+s(e_\zeta,-f).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.24}
\]

Convexity of the cone, and membership of
\((-e_\zeta,f)\) in it, proves that the complement is
preserved by the same argument as OCM.7. The coefficient
in HI.19 is constant in \(\zeta\). OCM.11 therefore
contracts the relative complex on the whole tangent ball
and its complement. This proves vanishing off the
conormal, with actual support refinements and finite
primitives. It does not use a wave-front theorem as an
external input.

#### HI.7. Every finite meromorphic pole gives an actual class

Let \(F\) be a holomorphic line with nonvanishing frame
\(\eta\), and let \(q\) be holomorphic on a connected
coordinate domain. For an integer \(j\ge1\), the
function \(q/f^j\) is holomorphic on the complement of
every support in HI.21. Its positive relative class is

\[
 \left(0,-\frac{q\eta}{f^j}\right).
 \tag{HI.25}
\]

This class is zero exactly when \(q/f^j\) extends
holomorphically across \(S\) on a smaller full domain.
Indeed the degree-zero part of the support exact
sequence identifies the kernel of the connecting map
with the image of full-domain holomorphic sections.
Equivalently, in a nonnegative injective model, a
degree-zero primitive for HI.25 is a closed degree-zero
section and hence a genuine holomorphic section.
No acyclicity of the domain or its complement is used.

If such an extension \(g\) exists, then \(f^jg=q\)
on a nonempty open subset. The holomorphic identity
theorem makes this equality hold on the connected
full domain. Conversely that equality supplies an
extension. Thus the kernel is precisely the
holomorphic part of \(F[1/f]\).
The same argument holds after every admissible
restriction or support enlargement: use a further
common cone HI.20, whose complement contains a
nonempty open set. In particular nonzero finite
principal parts cannot disappear in the filtered
microlocal colimit.

Theorem HI.B therefore gives, on every nonzero
conormal stalk, an injection

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \frac{F[1/f]}{F}\\
 \longrightarrow
 H^0\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbb C_S[-1],F).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.26}
\]

It is compatible with restrictions, real phases and
holomorphic frame changes. Each germ is represented
by the same finite meromorphic expression; finite
equalities use one common support domain. For \(q=1\)
and \(j=1\), the class is nonzero at every phase.
Its one-normal residue is

\[
 \frac1{2\pi i}\int_{|f|=\epsilon}\frac{df}{f}=1.
 \tag{HI.27}
\]

The parametrization \(f=\epsilon e^{it}\) proves
HI.27 directly. This is the hypersurface normalization;
it is not a degree-\(N\) diagonal inverse-product
calculation.

Under the open/closed isomorphism OCM.22, HI.25 is
the connecting image of the meromorphic complement
section. To check its sign, choose an injective
extension \(b\) of that section. The Hom connecting
map sends it to \(db\). In the relative convention,
\((0,-q\eta/f^j)+d(b,0)=(db,0)\).
Thus OCM.20 and the positive sign in HI.25 agree.

#### HI.8. The full finite differential-operator pole model

Trivialize \(F\) by \(\eta\), and let differential
operators act on its scalar coefficient. This is
a local trivialized action; no global flat connection
on the coefficient line is asserted.
Write \(\mathcal D\) for finite-order holomorphic
operators in \((z,f)\). Its operators have the
finite normally ordered form

\[
 P=\sum_{\alpha,k}a_{\alpha,k}(z,f)
                    D_z^\alpha D_f^k.
 \tag{HI.28}
\]

Repeated Leibniz differentiation proves closure and
normal ordering. Uniqueness follows by applying an
alleged zero operator to
\(e^{\langle\lambda,z\rangle+\mu f}\):
the resulting polynomial in the constant parameters
\((\lambda,\mu)\) has every coefficient zero.
Thus no formal or infinite differential sum is involved.

Let \(e\) denote the class of \(\eta/f\). Then

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 fe=0,\qquad D_{z_i}e=0,\\
 D_f^ke=(-1)^kk!\frac{\eta}{f^{k+1}}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.29}
\]

These identities hold in the finite-pole quotient and,
by HI.26, in the actual microlocal Hom class.
Naturality in the coefficient sheaf makes HI.26
linear for every finite differential-operator map.

The exact cyclic presentation is

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \frac{\mathcal D}
 {\mathcal D f+\sum_i\mathcal D D_{z_i}}\\
 \simeq\frac{F[1/f]}F.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.30}
\]

Here all ideals are left ideals; their displayed
generators occur on the right of an arbitrary operator.
For the proof, every term of HI.28 with \(\alpha\ne0\)
has a rightmost tangent derivative and is in the
displayed ideal. For the remaining terms use
\(fD_f^k=D_f^kf-kD_f^{k-1}\). Its finite iteration gives

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f^jD_f^ke\\
 =(-1)^j\frac{k!}{(k-j)!}D_f^{k-j}e,\\
 0\le j\le k;\\
 f^jD_f^ke=0,\quad j>k.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.31}
\]

Expand each holomorphic \(a_{0,k}(z,f)\) only through
degree \(k\) in \(f\), with a holomorphic remainder
divisible by \(f^{k+1}\). Taylor's formula in one
convergent coordinate gives that finite division.
HI.31 reduces every operator class to
\(\sum_{\ell=0}^K b_\ell(z)D_f^\ell e\).
If its meromorphic class is zero, uniqueness of the
finite Laurent principal part makes every \(b_\ell\)
zero. This proves injectivity in HI.30.
For surjectivity, the finite principal part
\(\sum_{\ell=0}^{j-1}c_{\ell+1}(z)\eta/f^{\ell+1}\)
is the image of
\(\sum_{\ell=0}^{j-1}(-1)^\ell c_{\ell+1}(z)
D_f^\ell/\ell!\).
This also proves that the whole finite-pole quotient,
not just individual pole orders, is represented.

The induced order filtration has normal basis
\(D_f^\ell e\), with \(\ell\le k\) in order \(k\).
Multiplication by \(f\) lowers that order; a tangent
derivative differentiates \(b_\ell(z)\) and does not
raise it. Consequently

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{gr}
 \left(\mathcal D/
   (\mathcal D f+\sum_i\mathcal D D_{z_i})\right)\\
 =\mathcal O_S[\tau_f].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.32}
\]

as a module over
\(\mathcal O_M[\xi_z,\tau_f]\). The annihilator is
exactly \((f,\xi_z)\), since the displayed polynomial
module is free in the normal variable.
This ideal is reduced: its quotient is a polynomial
ring over the convergent coordinate ring on \(S\),
which is a domain by the lowest nonzero homogeneous
term argument for convergent power series.
The support is the full conormal, and the principal
generator is the unit of this quotient.

**Theorem HI.C.** The actual all-phase class of
\(\eta/f\) contains the entire finite cyclic
differential-operator module HI.30 injectively.
Its associated graded module is HI.32, with the
reduced conormal ideal and the unit principal
generator. This includes \(m=1\), with an empty
tangent-derivative list.

**Proof.** HI.25–HI.27 proves injectivity in the
source-defined support colimit, and HI.B transfers
it to microlocal Hom with its explicit shift.
HI.28–HI.32 proves the exact finite presentation
and filtration on the same class. \(\square\)

Changing a nonvanishing frame conjugates the local
coefficient action by its holomorphic unit. It changes
the displayed generator by that unit and identifies
the two injected modules and their filtered presentations.
Their reduced principal support is the same.
HI.C does not infer cyclic generation by the full
finite microlocal ring from the differential-operator
presentation, or apply an unproved extension-flatness
or elliptic-regularity assertion.

#### HI.9. Incidence and the two operator sides

For the incidence pair, \(N=d+1\), \(m=2N\), and

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f=s-t-x^{\mathsf T}y,\\
 \eta=ds\wedge dy_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dy_d.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.33}
\]

The coordinate change to \(f\) has input Jacobian one:
with the output variables fixed,
\(\eta=df\wedge dy_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dy_d\).
Thus it retains the ordered input frame and does
not insert an additional density scalar.
The nonzero conormal \(-\tau\,df\), with the input
antipodal operation, is exactly the Legendre graph
computed in [LI.4](#5-57-legendre-incidence-and-the-topological-inverse-of-projective-duality). Theorem HI.C gives a genuine
holomorphic microlocal Hom class there at every phase.

The literal function identities [LI.20](#5-57-legendre-incidence-and-the-topological-inverse-of-projective-duality) consequently
descend to this actual class. For \(K=\eta/f\),
acting on scalar coefficients in the displayed frame,
they are

\[
 \begin{gathered}
 -D_sK=D_tK,\\
 y_iD_tK=D_{x_i}K,\\
 D_{y_i}K=x_iD_tK,\\
 (s-t)D_tK\\
 =K+\sum_i x_iD_{x_i}K.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HI.34}
\]

The input derivative has the negative transpose in
the ordered input-density convention. The last
relation corresponds to the simple-pole parameter
\(\alpha=0\) in [LI.21](#5-57-legendre-incidence-and-the-topological-inverse-of-projective-duality). It remains a cleared relation:
no primitive defining \(D_t^{-1}K\) on holomorphic
functions has been chosen.

The finite-\(E\) simple-generator identification,
both normalized inverse cup/excision/trace products,
compatibility with the entire LN maps and the action
on arbitrary RM.3 real-kernel representatives are
additional requirements. In particular the reduced
finite-\(\mathcal D\) characteristic ideal in HI.32
does not by itself identify a full \(E\)-bimodule
or a whole-real inverse. The arbitrary-holonomic
regularization and analytic proper/Riemann–Hilbert
arguments retain those hypotheses.

Free primary context is
[Benchoufi, Action of micro-differential operators on quantized
contact transformations, arXiv:2102.08861v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.08861v2),
§§3.2 and 4.3–4.5. The shrinking support comparison,
its polar sign, actual pole-class injection and finite
operator presentation used here are proved in HI.0–HI.9
and the exact earlier programme sections cited above.

### 5.61. The finite microlocal hypersurface module

Let \(M\) have complex dimension \(m\ge1\), let \(S=\{f=0\}\)
be a smooth hypersurface, and use coordinates
\((z,f)\), \(z\in\mathbb C^{m-1}\). Work near a nonzero
conormal with normal covariable \(\lambda\ne0\), and put
\(w=\xi_z/\lambda\). Write \(E\) for the actual finite-order
microlocal ring of §§5.19–5.22. A symbol has the form
\[
 P=\sum_{j\le b}p_j(z,f,w)\lambda^j.
 \tag{FIM.1}
\]
There is one common coefficient product. On each smaller
compact product its negative coefficients obey
\(\|p_{-n}\|\le MC^n n!\). The finite upper bound \(b\)
belongs to the whole operator. All sums below mean actual
coefficient sequences with these bounds, rather than
convergent numerical Laurent sums in \(\lambda\).

The ring, its products and ordinary changes of coordinates
are the actual constructions of §§5.19–5.22, §5.28 and
§5.56. Their finite matrix-kernel coherence is §5.24 and
§5.31, L.5–L.6. The normal-coordinate Koszul contraction
is §5.54, EE.5–EE.9. The actual halfspace action and its
normal primitive gauges are §5.53, AM.B–AM.C. The
hypersurface support convention and pole class are
§5.60, HI.1–HI.32.

The exact earlier programme proof dependencies are [§5.19](#5-19-actual-factorial-growth-symbols-and-ordered-jets), [§5.32](#5-32-coherent-actual-lattices-and-principal-support-for-the-whole-germ), [§5.43](#5-43-the-canonical-all-degree-action-and-its-derived-module-structure), [§5.52](#5-52-full-euler-matrix-division-and-comparison-reductions), [§5.53](#5-53-real-kernel-comparison-for-all-constant-euler-matrices), [§5.54](#5-54-halfspace-solutions-and-finite-euler-extensions), [§5.56](#5-56-whole-real-kernel-coordinate-transport-and-balanced-comparison), [§5.57](#5-57-legendre-incidence-and-the-topological-inverse-of-projective-duality), [§5.58](#5-58-full-analytic-legendre-transport-and-quadratic-factorization), [§5.59](#5-59-open-and-closed-incidence-in-the-actual-microlocal-hom-complex), [§5.60](#5-60-the-holomorphic-incidence-class-and-shrinking-normal-supports), [EC.B](#ec-b-the-actual-opposite-ring-and-right-finiteness).

#### FIM.0. The entire cyclic quotient

Consider the finite presentation
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathcal M_S=\\
 E/(Ef+\sum_i ED_{z_i}),\\e=[1].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.2}
\]
The ideals are left ideals. In particular the annihilating
coordinate or derivative is on the right of a coefficient
operator. This quotient is coherent by the actual finite
matrix-kernel theorem. It is a quotient of the entire
actual \(E\), with its infinite negative tail retained.

We prove a strict normal form for FIM.2:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 Q=\sum_{j\le b}q_j(z)\lambda^j,\\
 \|q_{-n}\|\le M'C'^n n!.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.3}
\]
Every class has exactly one such row. The reduction does
not increase its upper order.

First divide the holomorphic coefficients of FIM.1 by
the commuting normal coordinates \(w_i\):
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 p_j(z,f,w)-p_j(z,f,0)\\
 =\sum_i w_i b_{j,i}(z,f,w).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.4}
\]
One explicit choice is
\(b_{j,i}=\int_0^1(\partial_{w_i}p_j)(z,f,sw)\,ds\).
The radial segment lies in the chosen inner polydisc.
A fixed outer Cauchy margin bounds the derivative by a
constant times the original coefficient norm.
Right multiplication by \(D_{z_i}\) is multiplication of
the normal symbol by \(\lambda w_i\). Hence FIM.4 subtracts
an element \(\sum_i B_iD_{z_i}\), where \(B_i\) has upper
order at most \(b-1\) and the same factorial type on one
smaller product. This is also the degree-zero augmentation
of the actual contraction EE.7.

Set \(a_j(z,f)=p_j(z,f,0)\), and choose an outer
\(f\)-disc of radius \(R>0\). Write its actual Taylor
coefficients as
\[
 a_j(z,f)=\sum_{k\ge0}a_{j,k}(z)f^k.
 \tag{FIM.5}
\]
Put \(a_j=0\) for \(j>b\), and use
\((j)_k=j(j-1)\cdots(j-k+1)\), with \((j)_0=1\).
Define
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 q_\ell\\
 =\sum_{k=0}^{b-\ell}(-1)^k(\ell+k)_k a_{\ell+k,k}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.6}
\]
For every output degree this sum is finite. In particular
it does not require a common domain for infinitely many
new Taylor remainders chosen separately.

The identity \([D_f,f]=1\) gives
\[
 fD_f^j=D_f^jf-jD_f^{j-1}
 \tag{FIM.7}
\]
for every integer \(j\). For negative \(j\), multiply the
identity for \(D_f^{-1}\) by finite inverse powers;
the normal inverse already belongs to \(E\).
Iterating FIM.7 gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f^kD_f^j\\
 =\sum_{\nu=0}^{k-1}(-1)^\nu(j)_\nu\\
 {}\cdot f^{k-1-\nu}D_f^{j-\nu}f\\
 {}+(-1)^k(j)_kD_f^{j-k}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.8}
\]
For \(k=0\) the sum is empty. Thus the candidate remainder
is exactly FIM.6.

Here are estimates for the entire division, including its
quotient. For \(r\ge1\), the Cauchy coefficient bound is
\[
 \|a_{-r,k}\|\le MC^r r!R^{-k}.
 \tag{FIM.9}
\]
For a negative output degree \(\ell=-n\), all terms of
FIM.6 with \(k\ge n\) vanish. Indeed \(j=k-n\ge0\)
and \(k>j\), so \((j)_k=0\). The nonzero terms give
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 q_{-n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
 \frac{(n-1)!}{(n-k-1)!}\\
 {}\cdot a_{-(n-k),k}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.10}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \|q_{-n}\|\le M(n-1)!\\
 {}\cdot\sum_{r=1}^n rC^rR^{-(n-r)}\\
 \le Mn!(C+R^{-1})^n.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.11}
\]
The last inequality follows by \(r\le n\) and by comparing
each term with the corresponding nonnegative binomial
expansion coefficient, which is at least one.
The finitely many nonnegative output degrees have only
finitely many contributing nonnegative input degrees.

The right-\(f\) quotient in FIM.8 is the actual symbol
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 A_\ell(z,f)\\
 =\sum_{\nu=0}^{b-\ell}(-1)^\nu(\ell+\nu)_\nu\\
 {}\cdot\sum_{k\ge\nu+1}
                 a_{\ell+\nu,k}(z)f^{k-1-\nu}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.12}
\]
On a fixed inner disc \(|f|\le r_0<R\), its inner
Taylor sum has norm at most
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \frac{MC^r r!R^{-(\nu+1)}}{1-r_0/R},\\
 \ell+\nu=-r<0.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.13}
\]
For \(\ell=-n\), only \(0\le\nu\le n-1\) contributes,
by the same falling-factorial zero. Hence
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \|A_{-n}\|\le\frac{M}{R(1-r_0/R)}\\
 {}\cdot n!(C+R^{-1})^n.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.14}
\]
The upper order of \(A\) is at most \(b\). All its other
coefficients involve finitely many outer holomorphic
coefficients. The infinite Taylor sums in FIM.12 converge
uniformly on the chosen inner product, with geometric
tails; fixed derivatives follow on one further product.
The coefficient identities FIM.8 can therefore be summed,
and prove the actual decomposition
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 P=Q+A f\\
 {}+\sum_i B_iD_{z_i}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.15}
\]
This is an equality in \(E\), with a common coefficient
domain and an explicit upper order for every term.

#### FIM.1. Uniqueness, filtration and the reduced conormal

Denote the remainder operation FIM.4–FIM.6 by \(N\).
It kills right multiples of every \(D_{z_i}\), since
their symbols vanish at \(w=0\). It also kills right
multiples of \(f\). After evaluation at \(w=0\),
the degree-\(j\) coefficient of \(Af\) is
\[
 f a_j+(j+1)a_{j+1}.
 \tag{FIM.16}
\]
Before evaluation the extra term in the fixed-\(\xi_z\)
normal derivative is \(-w\cdot\partial_w a_{j+1}\),
which vanishes at \(w=0\).
Substitution of FIM.16 into FIM.6 cancels adjacent
Taylor indices: the contribution of \(fa_j\) at
index \(k\ge1\) has the opposite sign from the
contribution of \(j a_j\) at index \(k-1\), and
\((j)_k=j(j-1)_{k-1}\). These are finite sums at
every output degree. Finally \(N(Q)=Q\) for a row
independent of \(f,w\). Thus FIM.15 proves uniqueness,
and
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \ker N\\
 =Ef+\sum_i ED_{z_i}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.17}
\]

Use the quotient order filtration from \(E\). FIM.15
keeps \(A\) in order \(b\), \(B_i\) in order \(b-1\),
and \(Q\) in order \(b\). Thus this is a strict
presentation, not merely a set-theoretic normal form.
Its order-\(b\) graded part is exactly
\[
 \operatorname{gr}_b\mathcal M_S
       =\mathcal O_S\lambda^b.
 \tag{FIM.18}
\]
The coefficient \(q_b\) vanishes precisely when the
normal row has order at most \(b-1\).
Multiplication by \(f\) lowers order, since
\[
 f(q_jD_f^je)=-j q_jD_f^{j-1}e.
 \tag{FIM.19}
\]
A tangent derivative gives
\(D_{z_i}(q_jD_f^je)=(\partial_{z_i}q_j)D_f^je\),
and hence has zero degree-one symbol on the quotient.
The full principal annihilator is therefore
\[
 I_{\mathcal M_S}=(f,\xi_z).
 \tag{FIM.20}
\]
There are no further principal equations, by FIM.18
and the arbitrary choice of its holomorphic coefficient.
The quotient coordinate ring on \(S\), with the
nonzero normal direction retained, is reduced: its
local convergent power-series ring is a domain by
the lowest nonzero homogeneous-term argument.
The order-zero quotient is generated by \(e\),
and \(D_f^{-1}\) acts injectively by shifting its
unique normal row. The actual support equality
J.3–J.4 of §5.32 therefore identifies its support
with the full conormal support of its principal
quotient, including every nearby stalk.
Thus FIM.2 with generator \(e\) is an actual coherent
simple microlocal module in the explicit sense of a
reduced principal annihilator equal to the ideal of
its conormal support.

#### FIM.2. Its convergent pole and logarithm representative

Let \(F\) be trivialized by a degree-zero holomorphic
frame \(\eta\). For every integer \(j\), use the
one-variable representatives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 u_j(f)=(-1)^j j!f^{-j-1},\\
 j\ge0,\\
 u_{-n}(f)=\frac{f^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}\\
 {}\cdot(\log f-H_{n-1}),\\
 n\ge1.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.21}
\]
where \(H_k=\sum_{\nu=1}^k1/\nu\), \(H_0=0\).
Choose the logarithm on the complement of a strict
closed positive-polar sector, as in HI.20–HI.21.
Differentiation and
\(H_k-H_{k-1}=1/k\) give
\(u_j'=u_{j+1}\), including \(j=-1\).
Modulo full-disc holomorphic functions,
\(fu_j=-j u_{j-1}\). For \(j=-n<0\), the difference
is exactly \(f^n/n!\); for \(j=0\), it is the
constant \(1\). These are actual holomorphic gauges.

For a normal row FIM.3, put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 U_Q(z,f)\\
 =\sum_{j\le b}q_j(z)u_j(f).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.22}
\]
This is an actual holomorphic function on the
sector complement on one fixed smaller product.
Indeed, on compact subsets of its punctured normal
disc, the negative-index summands are bounded by a
constant times
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 n C'^n|f|^{n-1} B_n,\\
 B_n=|\log f|+1\\ {}+\log(n+1).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.23}
\]
Choose the normal radius before summing, so that
\(C'|f|<q<1\). The sum converges normally, with
summable geometric-polynomial tails and all fixed
derivatives on further compact margins.
The harmonic-number part alone converges on a
full disc, as a holomorphic gauge.

Its logarithmic coefficient is the genuine function
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 A_Q(z,f)\\
 =\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{q_{-n}(z)f^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.24}
\]
Changing a logarithm branch changes FIM.22 by a
constant integer multiple of \(2\pi i A_Q\).
That function is holomorphic on the full small
product. Thus FIM.22 determines a branch-independent
actual relative class
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 Q\longmapsto[(0,-U_Q\eta)]\\
 \in H^1\mathfrak h_{f,p}(F).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.25}
\]
at every nonzero conormal phase \(p\).
The sign is the same as HI.25. Its restriction
for \(j\ge0\) is precisely the finite-pole injection
HI.26.

This map is injective. If FIM.22 agrees on a later
sector complement with a full-domain holomorphic
function, continue that equality around a normal
circle using finitely many overlapping angular
charts. The full-domain function is single valued.
The jump of FIM.22 is \(2\pi i A_Q\); hence the
actual function \(A_Q\) is zero. Its Taylor
coefficients kill every \(q_{-n}\). The remaining
finite negative Laurent principal part extends
holomorphically only if every \(q_j\), \(j\ge0\),
is zero, by circle coefficient extraction.
The same argument holds after every common support
refinement, and with arbitrary holomorphic \(z\)
parameters on a smaller product.

The map is linear for finite differential operators
and holomorphic scalar multiplication. For \(D_f\)
and \(D_z\), use FIM.21 and normal convergence.
For a general holomorphic scalar \(g(z,f)\),
FIM.10 shows that the logarithmic coefficient of
the normal remainder of \(gQ\) is exactly
\(gA_Q\), by the ordinary Cauchy product.
Its finite negative Laurent part is the actual
principal part of \(g\sum_{j\ge0}q_ju_j\).
All other terms extend on a full smaller disc by
the estimates FIM.9–FIM.14 and FIM.23.
This proves the stated scalar compatibility without
an infinite algebraic sum of operators.

Transporting the action of \(E\) on its quotient
FIM.2 through this injection gives an \(E\)-module
structure on its explicit pole/logarithm image.
FIM.4 identifies that structure with the actual
kernel cup/excision/trace action on the strict
hypersurface support complex.
Theorem HI.B identifies the underlying relative
classes with actual microlocal Hom classes.
FIM.5 identifies this action with the geometric
microlocal Hom action using the entire relative
cube and proper trace.

#### FIM.3. Rank one over the output algebra on the incidence chart

Let \(N=d+1\), \(M=X\times Y\), and choose
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f=s-t-x^{\mathsf T}y,\\
 z=(t,x,y).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.26}
\]
The relative input form \(ds\wedge dy_1\wedge\cdots
\wedge dy_d\) has input Jacobian one in these
coordinates, as in HI.33.
The actual module FIM.2 has the tangent annihilators
in the \(z\)-coordinates and normal covariable
\(\lambda=\xi_f\).

In the new coordinates the old output derivatives are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 D_t^{\rm old}=D_t^{\rm new}-D_f,\\
 D_{x_i}^{\rm old}=D_{x_i}^{\rm new}-y_iD_f.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.27}
\]
They commute with every \(y_i\), and commute with
each other. Consequently the full output normal
symbol
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 P=\sum_{j\le b}r_j(t,x,v)\tau^j,\\
 v=\xi_x/\tau.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.28}
\]
has normal remainder in \(\mathcal M_S\)
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 N(Pe)=\sum_{j\le b}(-1)^j\\
 {}\cdot r_j(t,x,y)\lambda^j e.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.29}
\]

To justify this for the entire actual symbol,
introduce the commuting normalized tangent
covariables \(\nu_0=\xi_t^{\rm new}/\lambda\),
\(\nu_i=\xi_{x_i}^{\rm new}/\lambda\).
The degree-\(j\) coefficient becomes
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 (\nu_0-1)^j\\
 {}\cdot r_j\!\left(t,x,\frac{\nu-y}{\nu_0-1}\right).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.30}
\]
There are no derivative corrections in this
commuting covariable substitution: the coefficients
of the transformed derivative fields are functions
of \(y\), while none of these fields differentiates
\(y\). Their normal ordering therefore agrees
literally with FIM.27.
More explicitly, the transformed symbols are
independent of \(f\) and of the new \(y\)-covariables.
In their actual Leibniz product the terms
differentiating \(f\) in the second factor vanish,
and the terms differentiating \(y\) have zero
covariable derivative in the first factor.
The remaining \(t,x\) contractions are exactly
the original output contractions, by the chain
rule in FIM.27. Thus the substitution preserves
the full actual product, not just polynomial
calibrations of its generators.
Choose one product with \(|\nu_0|<c<1\) and with
the displayed argument inside the original
covariable domain. Evaluation at \(\nu=0\)
is FIM.29. The remainder is divisible by the
commuting tangent covariables using the radial
division FIM.4, so is in their right-generated
left ideal.
For \(j=-n\), the extra factor has norm at most
\((1-c)^{-n}\). Thus the entire negative tail
still obeys one factorial estimate. The division
uses one additional Cauchy margin and lowers order
by one. All fixed derivatives and tails are on
these common products.

Conversely every normal row \(q_j(t,x,y)\) in
FIM.3 is FIM.29 for the actual output symbol
\(r_j(t,x,v)=(-1)^j q_j(t,x,v)\). The coefficient
domains and factorial bounds are identical after
renaming the variable.
Uniqueness in FIM.17 therefore proves the actual
filtered left-module isomorphism
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 E_X\longrightarrow\mathcal M_S,\\
 P\longmapsto Pe.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.31}
\]
This calculation includes \(d=0\) and every
negative order; it is not limited to polynomial
covariable coefficients or generator relations.

The commuting right input action, with its negative
transpose in the ordered input frame, satisfies
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 eD_s=D_t e,\\
 ey_i=D_{x_i}D_t^{-1}e,\\
 eD_{y_i}=-x_iD_te,\\
 es=\\
 (t+\sum_i x_iD_{x_i}D_t^{-1})e.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.32}
\]
These are algebraic identities in the actual cyclic
module. The normal inverse is the inverse in \(E\);
no primitive of a holomorphic function is selected
by FIM.32.
FIM.6 identifies the whole finite-order right input
action with LN.8–LN.24, including its common-domain
bounds. Its proof uses strict finite-degree dependence
and holomorphic finite jets in addition to FIM.32.

The canonical action comparison is FIM.5. Both
normalized inverse cup/excision/trace products are
separate assertions; the finite cyclic presentation
and the output rank-one algebra do not imply them.

#### FIM.4. The canonical action on strict hypersurface supports

We construct the action on the hypersurface support
side without presuming a microlocal Hom action
comparison. Rotate the ordinary \(f\)-coordinate
so that its selected positive polar is
\(\Re f>0\). Ordinary coordinate transport, with
the input Jacobian and orientation, is BCT.1.
The strict support sectors
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 H_L=\\
 \left\{\begin{gathered}
 a=\Re f\ge0,\\|\Im f|\le La
 \end{gathered}\right\}\\
 {}\times\mathbb C_z^{m-1},\\
 0<L<\infty.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.33}
\]
on shrinking products are cofinal by HI.20–HI.21.
Let \(C=\mathscr E^{\mathbb R}_p\) be the entire
source-defined real kernel stalk of AM.H.
For a finite list of kernel classes, relations
and boundary witnesses, that lemma supplies one
actual coefficient domain and one support cone
in the difference \(n=v-u\):
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 l=-\Re n_f\ge0,\\
 |\Im n_f|\le\epsilon l,\\
 |n_z|\le A l,\\ \epsilon,A<\infty.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.34}
\]
Choose \(L\) at least \(\epsilon\) and at least
each earlier sector aperture in the finite
diagram. Increasing a finite aperture keeps a
strict positive polar margin.

If \(v\in H_L\) and \(n=v-u\) belongs to FIM.34,
then \(u\in H_L\). More precisely,
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 0\le a_v\le a_u,\\
 l=a_u-a_v\le a_u,\\
 |\Im f_u|\\
 \le|\Im f_v|+|\Im n_f|\\
 \le La_v+\epsilon l\le La_u.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.35}
\]
Thus the projected support is the same \(H_L\).
Its complement is open in the required cone
direction: \(u\notin H_L\) and \(n\in G\)
implies \(u+n\notin H_L\), by the same
contrapositive implication.

The whole closed intersection is proper on one
smaller output domain. Above a compact output
set, FIM.35 bounds \(l\), while FIM.34 bounds
both the imaginary normal displacement and
every tangent displacement. First choose an
outer source box inside the coefficient domains;
then choose the output box small enough that
these closed bounds lie strictly inside it.
The intersection is closed in the resulting
compact source box. This proves properness
and supplies a single inner/outer collar.
For any finite product, the nonnegative lengths
add to \(a_u-a_v\le a_u\); all intermediate
variables satisfy the same bounds, with the
largest of the finitely many cone constants.
AM.H's actual round-domain refinement applies
on these boxes. No arbitrary restriction of
a proper support is used.

Use DLG.3's entire four-entry relative cup,
including both complement entries and their
double-complement entry. Apply its full-cone
augmentation, the proper collar DLG.15, and
the ordered trace DLG.16 over the middle
complex \(m\)-dimensional variable. The kernel
has degree \(m\), and the trace lowers degree
by \(m\); it therefore acts in every input
relative degree. The kernel complement sign
and trace signs are exactly DLG.3–DLG.4.
Their explicit homotopies retain the entire
input boundary primitive.

The entire eight-entry triple cube and
properness just proved give DLG.5's
associativity and positive diagonal unit on
this target. DLG.3 and DLG.7 compare a larger
sector, a larger finite cone list and a
smaller actual domain. Each equality has
finitely many representatives and witnesses,
so is realized at one later common index.
Taking their filtered colimit constructs a
unital canonical \(C\)-action on
\(\mathfrak h_{f,p}(\mathcal O)\), in every
degree. This argument uses arbitrary full
relative kernel representatives, not just
symbols or supported currents.

There is a natural support-enlargement map
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 H^1\mathfrak h_{f,p}(\mathcal O)\\
 \longrightarrow\\
 \underset{D}{\operatorname{colim}}\,
       H^1_{\{\Re f\ge0\}}(D;\mathcal O)\\
 =\mathcal S.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.36}
\]
The target is exactly AM.16 for the same
normal phase and difference direction.
The map is \(C\)-linear: both actions use
the same full relative cup, and the
support-enlargement maps commute with its
finite-cube augmentation. One common proper
collar compares both support-to-image roofs
by DLG.17 and the collar homotopy DLG.4.
The normalized trace is unchanged.

The map FIM.36 is injective in degree one.
Here is a proof that does not infer
injectivity of a general support-forgetting
map. On a product polydisc \(D\),
\(H^1(D;\mathcal O)=0\), by OC.2's explicit
strictly plurisubharmonic disc exhaustion
and the fully proved DLH existence theorem.
The support exact sequence therefore
represents every degree-one class by a
holomorphic function on \(D\setminus H_L\),
modulo a full-domain holomorphic function.
The complement is the product of the
tangent polydisc and a connected angular
sector of opening strictly less than
\(2\pi\); it contains the left half-disc.
If restriction of this function to a
smaller left half-polydisc agrees with a
full-polydisc holomorphic function, their
difference vanishes on that nonempty open.
The holomorphic identity theorem makes
the difference zero on the entire
connected smaller complement.
This is exactly a zero relative class.
Every witness was on an actual later
product, so the same argument proves
injectivity in the filtered colimit.

Let \(e_p\) be the actual positive relative
class of \(1/f\). The ordinary multiplication
and derivative calibration gives
\(fe_p=D_{z_i}e_p=0\).
The canonical action thus defines
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 E/(Ef+\sum_i ED_{z_i})\\
 \longrightarrow H^1\mathfrak h_{f,p}(\mathcal O),\\
 [P]\longmapsto Pe_p.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.37}
\]
To identify it on an entire normal row,
compose with FIM.36. The whole halfspace
action is AM.B. For the constant scalar
Euler parameter \(-1\), its detector is
\(E_{-1}=1/f\). AM.24–AM.25b and the
full-disc convergent primitive gauges
AM.23a–AM.23c identify the image of
\(\sum q_j(z)D_f^j\) with FIM.22.
This use involves the full negative
factorial tail; a finite sum of primitives
does not replace the actual calculation.
The two elements of the source of
FIM.36, namely \(P e_p\) and FIM.25,
have the same target. Injectivity of
FIM.36 makes them equal.
Injectivity of FIM.25 then proves that
FIM.37 is injective.

Consequently the actual pole/logarithm
image is an \(E\)-submodule for the
canonical support-side action, with the
strict simple presentation FIM.2 and
the output rank-one isomorphism FIM.31
on the incidence chart. Rotating back
gives the same statement at every
nonzero conormal phase.
FIM.5 proves that HI.B's topological
Thom comparison intertwines this action
with the composition action on microlocal
Hom. Its relative-cube/proper-trace
diagram retains the two eliminated normal
blocks and all their complement terms.
Both normalized holomorphic inverse
products and whole-real contact transport
are separate assertions.


#### FIM.5. The hypersurface Thom comparison and the canonical action

Use the conventions of FIM.0–FIM.4 and §5.60. In particular
\(M\) has complex dimension \(m\), \(S=\{f=0\}\), its tangent
coordinates are \(z\in\mathbb C^{m-1}\), and the selected
normal phase is \(\Re f>0\). The entire real kernel stalk
is \(C=\mathscr E^{\mathbb R}_p\). Its action means the
full relative cup, finite complement-cube augmentation,
proper excision and normalized holomorphic trace of
DLG.1–DLG.7. The same operations define composition on
microlocal Hom. No supported-current representative is
required.

Let
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Theta:\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbb C_S,\mathcal O_M)_p\\
 \longrightarrow\mathfrak h_{f,p}(\mathcal O_M).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.38}
\]
be the comparison HI.B. Its two normal maps are the
positive Thom maps HI.12–HI.18, with real dimensions
\(2\) and \(k=2m-2\); its projection shift is \([2m]\).
The tangent-normal map is the inverse of the
zero-support enlargement followed by its normalized
orientation trace. These specifications determine
\(\Theta\), including its sign.

We compare the two compositions in
\[
 \Theta(k\circ a)=k\cdot\Theta(a).
 \tag{FIM.39}
\]
Here \(k\) is any whole real kernel class, \(a\) is a
relative microlocal Hom class of any degree, \(\circ\)
is composition, and the action on the right is
FIM.4's action on strict hypersurface supports.
The letter \(k\) in this formula denotes a kernel;
the real tangent-normal dimension elsewhere is
explicitly written \(2m-2\).

Here is the composition map in the support model.
On the three-variable space, HI.19 identifies
the second factor's derived Hom from
\(\mathbb C_S(w)\) with sections supported on
\(f_w=0\) of the coefficient pulled back from
\(v\), with shift \([2m]\). Tensor that factor
with the kernel coefficient, whose input
top form is in \(v\). Ordinary coefficient
evaluation multiplies the \(v\)-holomorphic
function into that top form. The supports
intersect. Projecting away \(v\) and using
the normalized holomorphic trace gives
the output coefficient pulled back from
\(u\), still with the same shift \([2m]\).
This is evaluation of the derived Hom
followed by its adjunction trace.

The closed condition \(f_w=0\) is independent
of \(v\), so it commutes with that operation.
On injectives this assertion uses the literal
sections-with-support intersection identity
HI.16. For the proper projection it is
checked after the common collar: restriction
to the ordinary complement \(f_w\ne0\)
commutes with the same compact \(v\)-trace,
and the cone of that restriction is its
closed support functor. R.6–R.7 identifies
the injective and full-relative calculations.
Applying the diagonal support maps in the
two factors gives their two-support cube;
its augmentation, proper excision and
trace are precisely DLG.3–DLG.17.
Thus the microlocal Hom composition in
FIM.39 is this whole-cube map, with both
complement coordinates, rather than
an operation inferred from its value
on supported classes.

##### FIM.5a. The three-variable support

Write \(u,v,w\) for the output, middle and last
variables. The middle trace is over \(v\).
Fix a finite list of kernels, input cochains,
relations and boundary witnesses. AM.H and FIM.34
give one actual coefficient domain and one
negative-polar cone
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \ell=\Re f_u-\Re f_v\ge0,\\
 |\Im(f_v-f_u)|\le\epsilon\ell,\\
 |z_v-z_u|\le A\ell.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.40}
\]
Choose \(L\ge\epsilon\) large enough for all input
strict sectors. After applying the inverse of the
input HI.A comparison, the input is represented
on
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f_w=0,\qquad z_w=z_v,\\
 H_L(v)=\\
 \left\{\begin{gathered}
 \Re f_v\ge0,\\
 |\Im f_v|\le L\Re f_v
 \end{gathered}\right\}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.41}
\]
This is a use of an inverse comparison roof, not
a claim that an arbitrary cochain is literally
supported on its zero section. HI.10, HI.15 and
R.6–R.7 supply that roof and its finite witnesses.
Cup with the kernel is applied to every entry of
the roof.

Put \(a=\Re f_u\), \(b=\Im f_u\), and
\(d=z_v-z_u\), regarded as a vector in
\(\mathbb R^{2m-2}\). On the closed intersection
of FIM.40 with \(H_L(v)\),
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 0\le\Re f_v\le a,\\0\le\ell\le a,\\
 |b|\le La,\qquad|d|\le Aa.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.42}
\]
Choose \(L_*>0\) with
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 L_*^2>L^2+256A^2,\\
 \rho(u)=\\
 \sqrt{\max\{L_*^2a_+^2-b^2,0\}}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.43}
\]
The outer sector is
\(H_*=\{a\ge0,\ |b|\le L_*a\}\).
Its radius \(\rho\) is continuous and zero
outside that sector. On the cup support,
\[
 |d|\le\rho(u)/16
 \tag{FIM.44}
\]
when \(a>0\); when \(a=0\), all of
\(\ell,b,d,\rho\) are zero. Thus both normal
sections \(z_w=z_u\) and \(z_w=z_v\), and their
straight segment, lie in the outer tangent ball.
Shrink the actual output domain so that
\(\rho<R/2\), where \(B_R^{2m-2}\) is the
tangent-normal coordinate ball.

The properness estimate is uniform throughout
this comparison. All intermediate \(v\)'s have
normal displacement at most \(a\), imaginary
normal displacement at most \(\epsilon a\),
and tangent displacement at most \(Aa\).
First choose the outer coefficient boxes and
then the smaller output box. Their whole
closed intersection lies in one compact
middle box over each compact output set.
The extra normal section has displacement at
most \(\rho/16\). Moving it leaves \(u,v\)
unchanged. Hence it preserves that proper
middle support and its common collar.
For finitely many consecutive kernels,
their nonnegative normal lengths add to
at most \(a\), so the same argument uses
the largest of the finitely many constants.

##### FIM.5b. A normal isotopy including the collapsed fibre

We give the comparison of normal sections on
the entire closed family, including \(\rho=0\).
This does not use pullback of differential
forms by a nonsmooth radius.

On the full base \((u,v)\), replace \(d\) by
the continuous vector
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \widetilde d=0\quad(d=0),\\
 \widetilde d=d\min\left\{1,\frac{\rho}{8|d|}\right\}\\
 (d\ne0).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.45}
\]
It is zero where \(\rho=0\), has
\(|\widetilde d|\le\rho/8\), and equals
\(d\) on the closed cup support by FIM.44.
The same equality holds when all the
displacements collapse.

Let
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \chi(r)=1,\\0\le r\le1/4,\\
 \chi(r)=3/2-2r,\\
 1/4\le r\le3/4,\\
 \chi(r)=0,\\r\ge3/4.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.46}
\]
For the real tangent-normal variable
\(\zeta=z_w-z_u\) and \(0\le t\le1\), set
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Phi_t(\zeta)=\zeta\quad(\rho=0),\\
 \Phi_t(\zeta)=\zeta+t\widetilde d\,\chi(|\zeta|/\rho)\\
 (\rho>0).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.47}
\]
The perturbation has Lipschitz constant at
most \(2|\widetilde d|/\rho\le1/4\).
Consequently
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \frac34|\zeta-\zeta'|\\
 \le|\Phi_t(\zeta)-\Phi_t(\zeta')|\\
 \le\frac54|\zeta-\zeta'|.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.48}
\]
For completeness, surjectivity does not
require an inverse-function assertion.
Given \(y\), iterate
\(\zeta_{n+1}=y-t\widetilde d\chi(|\zeta_n|/\rho)\).
Successive differences decrease by a factor
at most \(1/4\). Their geometric sum
converges in Euclidean space to a solution;
the same contraction estimate proves
uniqueness. FIM.48 proves continuity of the
inverse, uniformly in the base and \(t\).
At \(\rho=0\), the displacement is at most
\(\rho/8\), for the map and its inverse.
Both therefore extend continuously there.

The maps are the identity for
\(|\zeta|\ge3\rho/4\). Points inside that
ball have image of norm at most
\(3\rho/4+\rho/8=7\rho/8<\rho\).
Bijectivity then shows that \(\Phi_t\)
preserves the closed ball of radius
\(\rho\), and its complement, in both
directions. It is also the identity near
the boundary of the fixed ball \(B_R\).
Moreover
\[
 \Phi_t(0)=t\widetilde d.
 \tag{FIM.49}
\]
Thus FIM.47 is a base-preserving isotopy
of the whole outer support and its
complement, taking the zero section to
the section \(d\) on the actual cup
support. Its inverse pullback transports
the positive zero-section Thom map to
that section's Thom map.

Here the coefficient complex, after cup
and the \(f_w\)-normal comparison, is
pulled back from \((u,v)\). It may be
the full derived-support coefficient
complex on the intersection of FIM.40
and \(H_L(v)\). HI.1 applies to every
such bounded complex. Apply its interval
projection comparison to the whole
domain and to its complement. The
restriction squares commute; taking their
relative cones proves that the two
endpoint maps induce the same map after
normal pushforward with support in the
outer ball. The inverse Thom maps at
the two normal sections therefore agree
after enlargement to that ball.

One can use an actual complex supported
on the closed base intersection: apply
the injective sections-with-support
functor before pulling back the normal
coordinate. Its sheaves are closed
direct images from that intersection,
so the equality \(\widetilde d=d\)
there is sufficient. No equality on an
unrelated open complement is presumed.

Every \(\Phi_t\) is isotopic to the
identity through these same maps.
Its normal orientation class is
therefore the positive one of HI.12–HI.15.
The isotopy does not multiply that class
by a nonzero scalar or reverse its sign.
When \(m=1\), the tangent-normal space
has dimension zero; all maps above are
the identity of the empty normal tensor.
