##### FIM.5c. The entire cup and proper trace

We now apply the normal-section comparison
to the full relative cup. If the kernel
is \((a,b)\) and the input is \((c,e)\),
DLG.3 uses its whole-domain entry, its
two single-complement entries and its
double-complement entry. The Thom maps
are coefficient maps on each of these
four entries. Restriction to every
ordinary complement commutes with them.
The finite cover augmentation and its
inverse are the maps DLG.5–DLG.14.
Thus the preceding comparison commutes
with that augmentation by DLG.14's
specified homotopy, rather than by
discarding either complement entry.
For a product or a relation, use the
corresponding eight-entry cube and
its same finite augmentation.

Before the middle trace, the coefficient
complex and both normal blocks are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \text{a complex on }(u,v),\\
 \text{the positive}\\
 f_w\text{-normal class},\\
 \text{the positive tangent}\\ \text{class}\\
 \text{at }z_w=z_v.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.50}
\]
Move the last normal section by FIM.5b
to \(z_w=z_u\) inside the outer
microlocal support. Now both normal
classes depend only on \(u,w\).
They can be placed outside the middle
trace over \(v\).

To justify this operation with the
excision roof, choose the middle
collar on the common compact
\((u,v)\)-support just proved proper.
Make it independent of \(\zeta\)
on \(|\zeta|\le R/2\); multiply by
a fixed outer normal cutoff equal
to one there if necessary.
Since \(\rho<R/2\) and \(\Phi_t\)
is the identity off the inner
normal support, this is a common
collar for the entire isotopy.
DLG.15 is applied to the augmented
full cone, including its derivative
of the cutoff and its complement
coordinate. The isotopy preserves
its actual proper support. DLG.14,
DLG.17 and the collar homotopy
therefore compare every choice
after one common finite refinement.

The trace commutation can also be
checked on the acyclic complexes.
Once the positive normal classes
are at the \(u\)-section, their
representatives and the inverse
normal comparison roof are
independent of \(v\). Relative
trace integrates the compact
\(v\)-coefficient. Exterior
product by the independent normal
class commutes with this integral
on each finite degree and every
complement entry. Properness
makes the integral a compact
one locally in \(u\).
V.4–V.6 and R.6–R.7 identify
this calculation with the
holomorphic/injective trace roof.
There is no pullback of the
holomorphic coefficient by
FIM.47: that coefficient depends
on \(u,v\), which the isotopy
fixes.

Both real normal dimensions are
even. Their total is \(2m\),
which cancels the projection
shift. Commuting the two normal
blocks contributes
\((-1)^{2(2m-2)}=1\).
If the input degree after
normal cancellation is \(q\),
the first relative trace sign
before cancellation is
\[
 (-1)^{m(q+2m)}=(-1)^{mq}.
 \tag{FIM.51}
\]
This is exactly DLG.16's sign
after cancellation. Its second
relative component has the
same additional factor
\((-1)^m\) on both sides.
The orientation of the
\(f_w\)-normal block is the
positive complex orientation;
the change \(f_w-f_u=-f_u\)
has positive real determinant,
as in HI.22. No additional
antipodal sign is introduced.

We have consequently constructed
a commuting diagram of actual
full-cube/proper-trace roofs.
On the first route, use the
input normal comparison,
compose the kernel and the
microlocal Hom class, and use
the output normal comparison.
On the second, apply the
canonical strict-support
kernel action. FIM.5b compares
the two possible normal
sections before tracing, and
the preceding computation
identifies every other map.
This proves FIM.39 in all
relative degrees.

Boundary representatives and
equality witnesses are retained.
For each finite diagram AM.H
supplies one common support
cone and coefficient domain;
DLG.14 and DLG.17 give the
comparison homotopies there.
Taking their filtered colimit
proves equality for the whole
real stalk \(C\), with no
finite-symbol or finite-tail
restriction.

The contravariant source shift
\(\mathbb C_S[-1]\) gives the
same comparison shifted by
\([1]\). Each entire operation
has degree zero after its
kernel degree and trace
degree cancel, so the common
shift contributes no new
action sign.

##### FIM.5d. The finite-\(E\) submodule in microlocal Hom

Combine FIM.39 with FIM.37.
The actual pole/logarithm
class defines an injective
map
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 E/(Ef+\sum_i ED_{z_i})\\
 \longrightarrow H^0\mu\operatorname{hom}\\
 (\mathbb C_S[-1],\mathcal O_M)_p.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.52}
\]
It is linear for the
canonical finite-\(E\)
action obtained by restriction
from \(C\). Its injectivity
is the injectivity proved
in FIM.2 and FIM.4, transported
through HI.B, not a
faithful-flatness assertion
about \(C/E\).
The strict filtration and
reduced conormal symbol ideal
are those of FIM.0–FIM.1.
On the incidence chart, the
output restriction of this
submodule is the rank-one
module FIM.31.

This statement concerns the
specified submodule and its
canonical action. It asserts
neither that its image is
the whole microlocal Hom
stalk nor that it is stable
under all of \(C\).
The infinite-order right input
Legendre comparison, both
normalized inverse
convolutions and general
holonomic regularization
are separate assertions.


#### FIM.6. The entire finite-order right input action

Use the incidence coordinates of FIM.3,
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f=s-t-x^Ty,\\
 z=(t,x,y),\\ \lambda=\xi_f\ne0.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.53}
\]
The ordered input form is \(ds\wedge dy\).
Right input operators act by their negative
transpose in that frame. The left output
operators commute with this action, since
their original variables are disjoint.
The input normal covariable \(\sigma\)
is nonzero on the selected conormal.

Ordinary coordinate transport of the
actual finite-order rings is §5.56.
The full transpose, obtained by moving
each input derivative across its
coefficient with its sign, is the actual
coefficientwise transpose of §5.51,
EC.B.1–EC.B.2, equations EC.B1–EC.B7.
These maps preserve upper
order and the negative factorial bound
on one smaller coefficient product.
No primitive of a holomorphic function
is part of this definition.

The support action comparison FIM.5
allows these input and output actions
on the specified microlocal Hom
submodule to be computed in
\(\mathcal M_S\). Its output
identification FIM.31 gives a map
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Phi:E_Y\longrightarrow E_X,\\
 eR=\Phi(R)e.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.54}
\]
Here the right-hand side is obtained
by applying the whole transposed input
operator in the ordinary incidence
coordinates, then the strict normal
division FIM.4–FIM.17 and the inverse
output identification FIM.29–FIM.31.
This constructs a whole actual map,
including its entire negative tail.
Each of those operations is
nonincreasing in upper order.

We prove
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Phi(R)=L_0(R),\\
 R\in E_Y.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.55}
\]
where \(L_0\) is the full Legendre
map LN.8–LN.24. The proof uses
finite jets of individual coefficients
and strictness; agreement on words
alone is not sufficient.

##### FIM.6a. Finite dependence of an output coefficient

Write
\[
 R=\sum_{j\le b}r_j(s,y,w)\sigma^j.
 \tag{FIM.56}
\]
For any integer \(q\), the difference
between \(R\) and its finite degree
slice
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 R_{\ge q}\\
 =\sum_{q\le j\le b}r_j(s,y,w)\sigma^j.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.57}
\]
has order at most \(q-1\).
If \(q>b\), the slice is zero.
Strictness of the three actual
operations defining FIM.54 shows
that the degree-\(q\) coefficient
of \(\Phi(R)\) is precisely that
of \(\Phi(R_{\ge q})\).
Strictness of LN.8–LN.24 gives
the same assertion for \(L_0\).

We also need continuity in the
holomorphic functions \(r_j\),
rather than just their degree
labels. In the input variables,
with \(t,x\) fixed as parameters,
the coordinate change is affine:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 s=f+t+x^Ty,\\
 D_s=D_f,\\
 D_{y_i}^{\rm old}=D_{y_i}^{\rm new}-x_iD_f.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.58}
\]
It substitutes \(w=\nu_y-x\)
in a homogeneous coefficient,
without a lower homogeneous
correction.

For the transpose, its ordinary
normal symbol is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 r^t(v,\xi)\\
 =\sum_\alpha\frac1{\alpha!}
       \partial_\xi^\alpha\partial_v^\alpha r(v,-\xi).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.59}
\]
This formula follows by repeatedly
using \((-D)a=-aD-\partial a\)
on a monomial; coefficient
uniqueness gives the displayed
normal symbol. For an input
homogeneous degree \(j\), the
term with index \(\alpha\)
has degree \(j-|\alpha|\).
Thus, among \(q\le j\le b\),
only finitely many indices
\(|\alpha|\le b-q\) can affect
degree \(q\).

The final normal division is
FIM.6. After the tangent
covariables are set to zero,
it uses only Taylor coefficients
in \(f\) with index at most
\(b-q\), and the coefficient
rows with degree at least
\(q\). Consequently the
degree-\(q\) coefficient of
FIM.54 is a finite sum of
restrictions and derivatives
of these finitely many
holomorphic \(r_j\)'s.
All evaluations take place
on one strictly smaller
coefficient product.
The Cauchy integral formula
on a fixed positive margin
proves continuity of this
finite expression for uniform
convergence on its outer
compact product.

The corresponding LN coefficient
is explicitly
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 (L_0R)_q=\\
 \sum_{K=0}^{b-q}(\mathcal A_Kr_{q+K})(\iota),\\
 \mathcal A_K=(-1)^K\\
 {}\cdot\sum_{|\gamma|=K}
       \frac{V^\gamma\partial_w^\gamma}{\gamma!},\\
 V_i=\partial_{y_i}+x_i\partial_s,\\
 \iota(t,x,z)=\\
 (t+x^Tz,z,-x).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.60}
\]
It is another finite continuous
jet expression on the same
kind of nested products.
The variable \(z\) in this
formula is the output
projective covariable.

##### FIM.6b. Polynomial coefficients and holomorphic coefficients

For polynomial coefficients in
\(s,y,w\), every term of
FIM.57 is a finite expression
in \(s,y,D_y,D_s,D_s^{-1}\).
The cyclic relations FIM.32
and commutation with the left
output action imply
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Phi(D_s)=D_t,\\
 \Phi(y_i)=D_{x_i}D_t^{-1},\\
 \Phi(D_{y_i})=-x_iD_t,\\
 \Phi(s)=\\
 t+\sum_i x_iD_{x_i}D_t^{-1}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.61}
\]
The inverse \(D_s^{-1}\) acts
as the actual inverse of its
action; in the output row it
is \(D_t^{-1}\).
Since the two sides commute,
\(e(R_1R_2)=\Phi(R_1)\Phi(R_2)e\).
FIM.31's injectivity makes
\(\Phi\) multiplicative.
LN.1–LN.8 gives exactly
the same ordered-word maps
for \(L_0\). Thus FIM.55
holds on the stated finite
polynomial expressions,
including negative powers
of the normal derivative.

Now fix \(q\) and a point of
the coefficient product.
Shrink to nested polydiscs
about the finitely many
evaluation points. Taylor
polynomials of each \(r_j\),
\(q\le j\le b\), converge
uniformly on the outer
compact polydisc and, by
one further Cauchy margin,
in every derivative occurring
in the two finite expressions.
Their polynomial identity
therefore passes to
the holomorphic coefficients.
The conclusion is equality
of the degree-\(q\)
holomorphic germs, throughout
their common inner product.
It is local in the base and
projective covariable and
hence holds on all the
chosen smaller product.

This is a coefficientwise
jet argument, not a proposed
convergence of numerical
Laurent series or a
polynomial approximation
to an entire negative tail.
The discarded lower-order
tail cannot enter degree
\(q\), by strictness.

##### FIM.6c. Actual negative tails

The construction of \(\Phi\)
already places its image
in the actual finite-order
output ring: transpose and
ordinary transport have
their fixed-product
factorial estimates, FIM.11
and FIM.14 give the strict
normal division estimate,
and FIM.31 preserves that
coefficient type. These
products can be nested
finitely many times,
independently of \(q\).

For \(L_0\), the estimate
LN.12 applied to FIM.60
is the entire negative-tail
estimate. In particular,
the terms with
\(q+K=-r<0\) have the
majorant
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 M\,\mathcal L^K K!\,C^r r!\\
 \le M\,n!\,\mathcal L^K C^r,\\
 K+r=n.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{FIM.62}
\]
where \(\mathcal L\) is
the fixed Cauchy contraction
constant of LN.12. Summing
them is bounded by
\(M n!(C+\mathcal L)^n\).
The finitely many
nonnegative input degrees
have their separate finite
coefficient norms; their
contribution is bounded
by \(M' C'^n n!\), since
a fixed polynomial in \(n\)
is bounded by an
exponential. There is
one finite upper order,
one common coefficient
product and one negative
factorial bound for the
whole output row.

The equality in every
degree proved in FIM.6b
therefore identifies two
actual germs with their
entire tails, proving
FIM.55. The complete
coefficient formula is
FIM.60, including arbitrary
holomorphic projective
covariable coefficients.

This proves the whole
finite-order input
identification. It does
not assert convergence
of normal division on a
symbol with infinitely
many positive degrees,
or identify the
infinite-order \(B\)
action merely from its
ordered generators.
Those assertions require
their own positive-tail
comparison. Both
normalized holomorphic
inverse products and
the full real contact
transport are also
separate assertions.


#### The finite-order incidence bimodule

**Theorem FIM.A.** At every nonzero conormal to a smooth hypersurface, the actual coherent quotient in FIM.2 injects into the shifted microlocal Hom in FIM.52, with its canonical finite-order action. The strict principal annihilator is the reduced conormal ideal. On the incidence chart its output restriction is free of rank one, generated by the single-pole class.

**Proof.** FIM.0–FIM.1 gives the strict coherent normal form and its principal annihilator. FIM.2 and FIM.4 prove injectivity of the pole/logarithm class for the actual strict-support action. FIM.5 transports it through the action-compatible HI.B comparison. The output rank-one assertion is FIM.31. All these constructions use one actual coefficient product for the entire finite-order symbol. \(\square\)

**Theorem FIM.B.** In the ordered incidence input frame, the entire finite-order right input action is the full Legendre isomorphism with parameter zero. In particular the specified incidence submodule is also free of rank one as a right input module.

**Proof.** FIM.6 identifies the actual right-input coefficient map with the whole map LN.8–LN.24. The latter is an algebra isomorphism by LN.4–LN.6. The output identification FIM.31 consequently identifies the map from the right input ring, sending an operator to its action on the single-pole class, with that isomorphism. It is a right-module isomorphism by the commuting left and right actions. \(\square\)

The rank-one bimodule statement is finite-order. It does not assert that the specified image equals the whole microlocal Hom stalk, or identify the full infinite-order or real operator actions. Normalized holomorphic inverse convolutions, general holonomic regularization and analytic proper regularity are separate statements.

Free primary context: [Benchoufi, *Action of micro-differential operators on quantized contact transformations*, arXiv:2102.08861v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.08861v2), especially Section 3. The arguments use the complete local proofs and exact earlier programme proof dependencies linked above.


### 5.62. The infinite-order incidence bimodule

The exact earlier programme proof dependencies are §§5.44, 5.51, 5.53, 5.58, 5.61, EC.B.

Use the actual rings \(E\subset B\subset C\) of §§5.53 and5.58.
In coordinates \((z,f)\) at a nonzero conormal, put
\(\lambda=\xi_f\ne0\), \(w=\xi_z/\lambda\). A whole
\(B\)-symbol has homogeneous coefficients on one common
product,
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 P=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}p_j(z,f,w)\lambda^j,\\
 \begin{cases}
 \|p_{-n}\|\le MC^n n!,&n\ge1,\\
 \|p_j\|\le M_\epsilon\epsilon^j/j!,&j\ge0.
 \end{cases}
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.1}
\]
with the second inequality for every \(\epsilon>0\).
The constants are for a fixed compact inner product;
that product is independent of the homogeneous index
and of \(\epsilon\). As in §5.58, these are actual
coefficient sequences, not numerical Laurent series
in \(\lambda\).

#### BI.0. The positive normal division

Consider
\[
 \mathcal M_B=B/(Bf+\sum_i BD_{z_i}).
 \tag{BI.2}
\]
The rightmost generators specify a left ideal.
The radial division FIM.4 removes the tangent
covariables. Its fixed Cauchy margin bounds the
dividing coefficients in both parts of BI.1.
Multiplication by \(\lambda^{-1}\) shifts their
index by one and retains both classes: for
positive indices use
\(\epsilon^{j+1}/(j+1)!\le
\epsilon\,\epsilon^j/j!\); the single new
negative coefficient is a fixed holomorphic
coefficient. Thus all tangent quotients are
whole \(B\)-symbols on a common product.

Write
\(a_j(z,f)=p_j(z,f,0)=\sum_{k\ge0}a_{j,k}(z)f^k\)
on an outer normal disc of radius \(R\).
For each nonnegative output index \(\ell\), define
\[
 q_\ell=
 \sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k(\ell+k)_k a_{\ell+k,k}.
 \tag{BI.3}
\]
This series is generally infinite. For every
\(0<\epsilon<R\), Cauchy's coefficient bound gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 |(\ell+k)_k a_{\ell+k,k}|\\
 \le M_\epsilon
       \frac{\epsilon^\ell}{\ell!}
                         (\epsilon/R)^k,\\
 \|q_\ell\|
 \le\frac{M_\epsilon}{1-\epsilon/R}
                      \frac{\epsilon^\ell}{\ell!}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.4}
\]
For a requested output parameter \(\delta>0\),
choose \(\epsilon\le\delta\) and
\(\epsilon<R/2\). BI.4 then proves the
every-\(\delta\) bound on the same inner
product. The sum and its fixed derivatives
converge normally, with geometric tails on
the chosen Cauchy margins.

For a negative output index \(-n\), every
nonnegative input degree in BI.3 has zero
falling factorial: if \(j=k-n\ge0\), then
\(k>j\). Consequently
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 q_{-n}=\\
 \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
 \frac{(n-1)!}{(n-k-1)!}a_{-(n-k),k},\\
 \|q_{-n}\|\le Mn!(C+R^{-1})^n.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.5}
\]
The positive input part contributes exactly
zero to every negative normal remainder.
This is an algebraic falling-factorial
identity, not a limiting cancellation
between unrelated coefficient domains.

The whole right-\(f\) quotient is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 A_\ell(z,f)=
 \sum_{\nu\ge0}(-1)^\nu(\ell+\nu)_\nu\\
 {}\times\sum_{k\ge\nu+1}
 a_{\ell+\nu,k}(z)f^{k-1-\nu}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.6}
\]
When \(\ell=-n\), all terms with
\(\nu\ge n\) are zero, so FIM.14 applies.
When \(\ell\ge0\), on \(|f|\le r<R\)
the absolute value of the \(\nu\)-term
is at most
\[
 \frac{M_\epsilon}{R(1-r/R)}
 \frac{\epsilon^\ell}{\ell!}
                         (\epsilon/R)^\nu.
 \tag{BI.7}
\]
Thus \(A\) satisfies the positive bound
of BI.1 for every output parameter and
the negative factorial bound of FIM.14.
There is one common product. Fixed
derivatives use one further fixed
Cauchy margin.

Sum the identity FIM.8 using these
absolute majorants. The tangent
quotients have already been constructed,
so it proves the entire identity
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 P=Q+Af+\sum_i B_iD_{z_i},\\
 Q=\sum_j q_j(z)\lambda^j.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.8}
\]
in the actual ring \(B\).

For uniqueness, evaluation at \(w=0\)
kills every right \(D_{z_i}\)-multiple.
The coefficients of a right \(f\)-multiple
are \(fa_j+(j+1)a_{j+1}\).
Substitution into BI.3 cancels the
two successive Taylor indices.
For \(\ell\ge0\), BI.4 andBI.7
make both series absolutely convergent;
their endpoint tails tend to zero
geometrically. For \(\ell<0\),
FIM.16 gives a finite cancellation.
The remainder of a row independent of
\(f,w\) is itself. Therefore BI.8 is
unique and its kernel is exactly
the left ideal in BI.2.

It also identifies
\(B\otimes_E\mathcal M_S\) with
\(\mathcal M_B\). Explicitly the map
sends \(b\otimes[P]\) to \([bP]\).
The inverse sends \([b]\) to
\(b\otimes[1]\); rightmost relations
go to zero by balancing. These are
inverse maps by the tensor relations.
No flatness of \(B/E\), \(C/E\) or
\(C/B\) is used.

#### BI.1. Entire normal functions

Use \(u_j\) of FIM.21, with its
positive connecting representative.
The negative part of
\[
 U_Q(z,f)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}q_j(z)u_j(f)
 \tag{BI.9}
\]
is the convergent logarithmic series
FIM.22–FIM.24 on a sufficiently small
punctured normal disc. On a compact
annulus \(|f|\ge r_1>0\), the
nonnegative summands satisfy
\[
 \|q_j u_j\|
 \le\frac{M_\epsilon}{r_1}
                    (\epsilon/r_1)^j.
 \tag{BI.10}
\]
Choose \(\epsilon<r_1/2\). This
proves normal convergence and all
fixed derivatives on that compact
annulus. Every compact subset of
the punctured product admits such
an estimate; the coefficient domain
and the punctured product do not
depend on \(j\). The nonnegative
part is single valued and may
have an essential singularity.

The branch jump remains exactly
\(2\pi i A_Q\), with \(A_Q\)
the full-disc holomorphic function
FIM.24. Hence the relative class
\([(0,-U_Q)]\) is branch independent.
If it extends holomorphically
on a full later product, continuation
around a normal circle gives
\(A_Q=0\) and kills every negative
coefficient. The remaining
nonnegative part is a normally
convergent Laurent series on that
circle. Termwise circle coefficient
extraction kills every \(q_j\),
\(j\ge0\). This proves injectivity
on the whole quotient BI.2,
including essential singularities.

The comparison with the canonical
action uses the same degree-one
support-forgetting injection
FIM.36. The whole AM.B halfspace
action for Euler parameter \(-1\)
has detector \(1/f\), and its
positive derivatives are exactly
the nonnegative \(u_j\)'s.
BI.10 is its actual convergent
positive part; FIM.23 is its
negative primitive part. The
normalization and holomorphic
gauges are AM.23a–AM.25b.
The two strict-support classes
therefore have the same halfspace
image; FIM.36 makes them equal.
FIM.5 transports this equality
to the canonical microlocal Hom
action. Thus BI.9 gives a
canonically \(B\)-linear
injection of the specified
quotient, without identifying it
with the entire microlocal Hom
stalk.

#### BI.2. Quantified positive cutoffs

The next comparison concerns
the input transpose and the
strict normal map. These have
to be controlled on a whole
positive tail before using
the finite-order identity.

Let \(P^{[J]}\) retain every
negative coefficient and the
nonnegative coefficients through
degree \(J\). The discarded
part has only positive degrees.
Fix \(0<\rho<1\). BI.4 gives
the following bound for its
nonnegative remainder:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \|N(P-P^{[J]})_\ell\|\\
 \le\frac{M_\epsilon\,\rho^{J+1}}
 {1-\epsilon/(\rho R)}
 \frac{(\epsilon/\rho)^\ell}{\ell!},\\
 \epsilon<\rho R.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.11}
\]
Indeed its summation indices
obey \(\ell+k>J\); extract
\(\rho^{\ell+k}\le\rho^{J+1}\)
and sum the remaining geometric
series. All its negative
remainders are zero by BI.5.
The quotient \(A\) has the
same extra geometric factor
in BI.7, with its additional
fixed factor \(1/[R(1-r/R)]\).

For the transpose, use the
two independent Cauchy margins
of EC.B3–EC.B5, and absorb the
number of derivative multi-indices
into a fixed constant \(D>0\).
A nonnegative input degree
\(m\) and derivative length
\(k\) contribute only to
output degree \(m-k\).
Their total norm is at most
\[
 M_\epsilon
       \frac{\epsilon^m}{m!}D^k k!.
 \tag{BI.12}
\]
The antipodal coordinate
neighbourhood contributes
a fixed exponential in \(m\);
choose a correspondingly
smaller input \(\epsilon\)
before applying BI.12.

For a nonnegative output \(j\),
write \(m=j+k\), and use
\(k!/(j+k)!\le1/j!\).
For a negative output \(-n\),
write \(k=m+n\), and use
\((m+n)!/m!=n!\binom{m+n}{n}\).
The elementary generating
identity
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \sum_{m\ge0}\binom{m+n}{n}x^m\\
 =(1-x)^{-n-1},\\
 |x|<1.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.13}
\]
follows by differentiating the
geometric series \(n\) times
and dividing by \(n!\).
Consequently the positive
input part of the transpose
has bounds
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \|(TP)_j^+\|
 \le\frac{M_\epsilon}{1-D\epsilon}
                         \frac{\epsilon^j}{j!},\\
 \|(TP)_{-n}^+\|
 \le\frac{M_\epsilon D^n n!}
                         {(1-D\epsilon)^{n+1}}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.14}
\]
These estimates construct the
actual whole transpose on \(B\).
The original negative part is
the actual EC.B transpose.

For the discarded positive
tail, the same extraction of
\(\rho^m\) proves
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \|T(P-P^{[J]})_j\|\\
 \le\frac{M_\epsilon\rho^{J+1}}
 {1-D\epsilon/\rho}
 \frac{(\epsilon/\rho)^j}{j!},\\
 \|T(P-P^{[J]})_{-n}\|\\
 \le\frac{M_\epsilon\rho^{J+1}D^n n!}
 {(1-D\epsilon/\rho)^{n+1}}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.15}
\]
Choose \(\epsilon<\rho/(2D)\).
The negative estimate then has
one factorial constant \(2D\)
independent of \(J\). For any
requested positive parameter
\(\delta\), also require
\(\epsilon\le\rho\delta\).
This proves an actual geometric
cutoff limit, simultaneously
for the negative class and
each positive seminorm, on
fixed nested coefficient
products.

BI.4 uses these estimates and
the full product majorants
IK.3–IK.10 to prove the actual
transpose anti-involution.
BI.6 gives the composite
transpose, affine coordinate
change and normal-division
cutoff estimate needed for
the entire input identification.

#### BI.3. A positive-tail example

For any complex parameter \(a\),
the actual symbol
\[
 P_a=\sum_{m\ge0}
           \frac{a^m f^m}{(m!)^2}D_f^m
 \tag{BI.16}
\]
belongs to \(B\). On \(|f|\le R\),
for every \(\epsilon>0\) the
ratio of its coefficient to
\(\epsilon^m/m!\) is bounded
by \(\exp(|a|R/\epsilon)\),
using the exponential series.
In BI.3 the only nonzero
output index is zero, and
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 N(P_a)_0=
 \sum_{m\ge0}\frac{(-a)^m}{m!}\\
 =e^{-a}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.17}
\]
Thus arbitrarily high positive
degrees can all contribute to
one output coefficient.
The geometric estimates are
essential to the whole quotient;
a finite-degree dependence
argument alone does not extend
FIM.6 to this class.


Use the domains and coefficient classes of BI.0–BI.3.
The actual binary and triple product majorants are
§5.44, IK.2–IK.3, equations IK.3–IK.10.
The finite transpose is §5.51, EC.B1–EC.B7.
The full Legendre map, including its cutoff estimates
and inverse, is §5.58, LN.4–LN.6.
The exact finite-order incidence module and both
finite-order operator sides are §5.61.

#### BI.4. The transpose is an actual anti-involution

We first specify the limiting assertion required
for the product proof. Suppose a family \(P_a\)
on a fixed coefficient product has common
negative bounds \(MC^n n!\), common positive
bounds \(M_\epsilon\epsilon^j/j!\) for each
\(\epsilon>0\), and coefficientwise normal
convergence with each fixed derivative.
Then \(T(P_a)\) has those same kinds of
common bounds on one fixed smaller product,
and converges coefficientwise normally,
with every fixed derivative, to \(T(P)\).

Indeed fix an output index \(j\).
The negative input indices which can enter
that output obey \(j\le m<0\), so there
are only finitely many. Their differential
expressions converge by the hypothesis.
For the nonnegative inputs, BI.12 gives
the same summable majorant for the entire
family: use the geometric series in
BI.14 when \(j\ge0\), or the binomial
series there when \(j<0\).
Choose its input \(\epsilon\) before
summing. Given a positive tolerance,
make the tail in the nonnegative input
index small using that common majorant.
The remaining finite sum converges
normally. A fixed further Cauchy margin
proves the same assertion for any
specified finite derivative.
BI.14 and the finite negative-part
EC.B5 estimate give the common growth
bounds. No coefficient-dependent
neighbourhood is used.

There is an analogous assertion for
products of such families. The proof
is contained explicitly in the scalar
majorants IK.3–IK.7: at a fixed output
degree the positive input indices,
absolute negative input indices and
contraction lengths satisfy the grouped
degree relation in IK.3. For common
input growth constants, choose a
common positive parameter making its
\(E(D+L)<1\). The scalar series is
summable. Its complement outside a
finite grouped-index range is uniformly
small by IK.6–IK.7. Inside that
range there are finitely many
holomorphic differential expressions,
which converge by hypothesis.
IK.8–IK.10 and one further Cauchy
margin give the assertion for the
products and all their fixed derivatives.
The same bounds give common positive
and negative output growth constants.

Now take the positive cutoffs
\(P^{[J]},Q^{[J]}\). They retain both
entire negative tails, so they belong
to the actual finite-order ring.
The finite transpose satisfies
EC.B6–EC.B7 there.
Their product family has common growth
bounds and converges normally,
coefficient by coefficient with fixed
derivatives, to \(P\circ Q\), by the
preceding product argument.
The transpose-family argument therefore
passes its left side to \(T(P\circ Q)\).

On the right, BI.14–BI.15 gives common
growth bounds and the corresponding
convergence of \(TP^{[J]}\) and
\(TQ^{[J]}\). The product-family
argument gives convergence to
\(TQ\circ TP\).
Taking the finite-order identity's
coefficient limit proves the second
identity below.
Apply the transpose-family argument
again to \(TP^{[J]}\).
The finite-order identities
\(T^2P^{[J]}=P^{[J]}\) tend to
the first identity. Its unit value
is immediate from the coefficient
formula. We have proved on whole
actual germs
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 T^2=1,\qquad T(1)=1,\\
 T(P\circ Q)=TQ\circ TP.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.18}
\]
The finite transpose is its restriction,
and every construction commutes with
sheaf restriction. The identities are
identities of actual holomorphic
coefficient sequences with the stated
growth bounds.

#### BI.5. The whole output module

On the incidence chart put
\(f=s-t-x^{\mathsf T}y\) and
\(z=(t,x,y)\). The ordered input
form is \(ds\wedge dy\).
Let \(e=[1]\) in BI.2.
The output map is the whole
coefficient substitution of FIM.30.
For an output normal symbol
\(\sum_j r_j(t,x,v)\tau^j\), its
normal row is exactly
\[
 \sum_j(-1)^j r_j(t,x,y)\lambda^j e.
 \tag{BI.19}
\]
This statement includes all positive
degrees as well as the complete
negative tail.

Here is the domain and product check.
On a compact product with
\(|\nu_0|<c<1\), the transformed
degree-\(j\) coefficient is FIM.30.
For \(j\ge0\), its extra factor is
bounded by \((1+c)^j\); choose
an input positive parameter divided
by \(1+c\) to obtain any prescribed
output parameter. For \(j=-n\),
the factor is bounded by
\((1-c)^{-n}\), which only enlarges
the fixed negative factorial constant.
The arguments of all coefficient
functions lie in one common original
product by the choice of the compact
output product.
The ordinary substitution is exact
because the transformed output fields
do not differentiate \(y\).
Every full contraction has the same
chain-rule cancellation as FIM.30;
IK.2–IK.3 justifies every sum and
regrouping on the fixed smaller product.
Equivalently the finite substitution
identities pass through the positive
cutoffs with these common scalar
majorants, retaining all negative
coefficients.

The transformed coefficients are
independent of \(f\). After radial
tangent division, the normal Taylor
formula therefore has only its
zeroth Taylor term. This proves
BI.19 directly. Its inverse renames
\(y\) as \(v\) and multiplies
degree \(j\) by \((-1)^j\).
It preserves both bounds on the
same renamed product. Consequently
\[
 B_X\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathcal M_B,
 \qquad P\longmapsto Pe
 \tag{BI.20}
\]
is an isomorphism of whole left
output modules. No upper order or
principal symbol is assigned to a
symbol with an infinite positive head.

#### BI.6. The entire right input map

Before changing the incidence
coordinates, whole output operators
and transposed input operators
commute. In either order, every
nonzero contraction would differentiate
a coefficient in a variable on
which it does not depend. Only the
ordinary coefficient product remains;
its scalar sums are absolute by IK.2.
The exact affine change preserves
that equality.
BI.18 therefore defines a right
\(B_Y\)-action commuting with
the left \(B_X\)-action on
\(\mathcal M_B\).

The affine input substitution, with
\(t,x\) held fixed as parameters, is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 s=f+t+x^{\mathsf T}y,\qquad
 \sigma=\lambda,\\
 w=\nu_y-x.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.21}
\]
It has relative input Jacobian one.
There is no density multiplier and
no lower homogeneous correction.
The argument is FIM.58 with actual
whole coefficients; the product-family
argument of BI.4 extends its finite
product identities. Choose nested
actual products such that every
displayed coordinate image lies
compactly inside its preceding
coefficient domain.

Via BI.20 define the whole map
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Phi_B:B_Y\longrightarrow B_X,\\
 eR=\Phi_B(R)e.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.22}
\]
Its calculation is: transpose the input,
apply BI.21, use the unique normal
remainder BI.3–BI.8, and invert BI.19.
Every operation has already been
constructed on actual whole symbols.

We give its composite cutoff estimate.
Fix \(0<\rho<1\), and put
\(R^{[J]}\) for the positive cutoff,
retaining the entire negative input
tail. Let \(Z^{[J]}\) be the affine
substitution of \(T(R-R^{[J]})\).
On the fixed substituted product,
BI.15 gives constants independent
of \(J\), with
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \|Z^{[J]}_{-n}\|\\
 \le K\,\rho^{J+1}(2D)^n n!,\\
 \|Z^{[J]}_j\|
 \le K_\epsilon\,\rho^{J+1}\epsilon^j/j!,\\
 j\ge0.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.23}
\]
For the first line choose one fixed
source parameter below \(\rho/(2D)\).
For each requested parameter in the
second line choose a further smaller
source parameter as in BI.15.
The normalizing input power is
\(\sigma=\lambda\), so BI.21 adds
no homogeneous exponential factor.
Fixed holomorphic parameter
substitution preserves these sup
bounds on the chosen compact products.

Let \(R_f>0\) be the outer normal
disc radius for the subsequent
normal division. BI.5 applied
to the first line of BI.23
gives the negative part of the
following estimate.
For its positive part use BI.4
with a parameter less than
\(R_f/2\) and at most the
requested output parameter
\(\delta\). Absorb its fixed
geometric denominator into the
prefactor. Inverting BI.19
only changes signs and renames
a holomorphic parameter.
Thus
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \|(\Phi_B(R)-\Phi_B(R^{[J]}))_{-n}\|\\
 \le K'\rho^{J+1}
                    (2D+R_f^{-1})^n n!,\\
 \|(\Phi_B(R)-\Phi_B(R^{[J]}))_j\|\\
 \le K_\delta'\rho^{J+1}\delta^j/j!,
 \qquad j\ge0.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.24}
\]
All products and margins precede
the indices and \(J\). Fixed
derivative versions follow on
one further product by the
iterated Cauchy formula. BI.24
is an actual coefficient and
tail estimate, rather than an
assumption about continuity of
microlocal cohomology.

For each \(J\), the symbol
\(R^{[J]}\) belongs to \(E_Y\).
Theorem FIM.B identifies its
right input action with
\(L_0(R^{[J]})\).
BI.24 passes the left side
coefficientwise normally to
\(\Phi_B(R)\).
LN.17–LN.18 and LN.6 passes
the right side, with its whole
negative actual tail retained,
to \(L_0(R)\).
Both coefficient sequences
are actual whole \(B_X\)
germs on the common product,
so
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Phi_B(R)=L_0(R),\\
 R\in B_Y.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.25}
\]
Since \(L_0\) is the whole
isomorphism of Theorem LN.C,
the map \(R\mapsto eR\)
also identifies \(\mathcal M_B\)
with the free rank-one right
input module.

#### BI.7. Positive-to-negative transpose mixing

In one spatial dimension choose
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 p_m(s,y,w)=\\
 \frac1{(m!)^2(1-y/2)}\\
 {}\times\frac1{1+w/2},\qquad m\ge0,\\
 p_m=0\quad(m<0).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.26}
\]
On \(|y|,|w|<1\) these are actual
whole coefficients: the rational
factor is uniformly bounded on
each compact, and
\(1/(m!\epsilon^m)\le e^{1/\epsilon}\)
proves the every-\(\epsilon\)
condition. This is the input
head of LN.32, now used to
compute the transpose itself.

There is no \(s\)-dependence.
Only the spatial contraction
of length \(K\) contributes
in the transpose formula.
At \(y=w=0,\sigma=1\),
the two differentiated
rational factors give
\((1/2)^K K!\) and
\((-1/2)^K K!\).
The antipodal substitution
also gives \((-1)^m\) on
homogeneous degree \(m\).
Since the output index is
\(j=m-K\), their total sign
is \((-1)^{m+K}=(-1)^j\).
Put \(c=1/4\). We obtain
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 (TP)_j(0)=\\
 (-1)^j\sum_{m\ge\max(0,j)}a_{j,m},\\
 a_{j,m}=\frac{c^{m-j}(m-j)!}{(m!)^2}>0.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.27}
\]
Every series converges by BI.14.
Thus every negative output
coefficient is nonzero, with
the indicated alternating
row sign. The antipodal sign
has been retained, not
discarded by projective
normalization.

For an integer \(J\ge|j|\)
let \(S_{j,J}\) be the
sum in BI.27 through \(m=J\).
For \(m\ge|j|\),
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \frac{a_{j,m+1}}{a_{j,m}}
 =\frac{m-j+1}{4(m+1)^2}\\
 \le\frac1{2(m+1)}\le\frac12,\\
 S_{j,J}<|(TP)_j(0)|\\
 \le S_{j,J}+2a_{j,J+1}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{BI.28}
\]
The inequality uses
\(m-j+1\le2m+1\le2(m+1)\).
Summing the positive omitted
terms against a geometric
series proves the enclosure.
These finite rational intervals
illustrate the full coefficient
map; the general ring and
input-action statements are
the independent arguments
BI.4–BI.6.

#### The infinite-order incidence bimodule

**Theorem BI.A.** The quotient BI.2
has the unique whole normal row
BI.3–BI.8 and is the algebraic
induced module \(B\otimes_E\mathcal M_S\).
Its normally convergent
pole/essential/logarithm representative
injects into the shifted hypersurface
microlocal Hom with the canonical
\(B\)-action. On the incidence chart
it is free of rank one over the whole
output ring and over the whole
right input ring. The input
coefficient map is the parameter-zero
Legendre isomorphism.

**Proof.** The normal row, its actual
growth bounds and the two inverse
balanced maps are BI.0. The injection
and its canonical action comparison
are BI.1, using the full action
compatibility FIM.5. BI.4 constructs
the actual input transpose and
proves its product identities.
BI.5 and BI.6 prove the two
rank-one identifications and their
whole input coefficient equality.
All positive cutoff limits retain
the entire negative tail.
\(\square\)

This theorem concerns the specified
induced module and its image. It
does not assert that its image is
the whole microlocal Hom stalk,
or that it is stable under every
real kernel in \(C\).
No general coherence theorem for
arbitrary \(B\)-modules, flatness
of \(C/B\), normalized holomorphic
inverse convolution, whole real
contact transport or arbitrary
holonomic regularization follows
from this rank-one computation.


Free primary context: [Benchoufi, *Action of micro-differential operators on quantized contact transformations*, arXiv:2102.08861v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.08861v2), Section 3. The complete arguments here use the exact earlier programme proofs linked above.


### 5.63. The opposite incidence kernel and its ordered periods

The exact earlier programme proof dependencies are §§5.56, 5.57, 5.58, 5.61, 5.62.

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) have complex dimension \(N=d+1\), with
coordinates \((t,x)\) and \((s,y)\), respectively. The spatial
number \(d\) may be zero. Use the actual rings and the entire
Legendre family of §§5.58 and5.62. Put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f=s-t-x^{\mathsf T}y,\\
 \eta_Y=ds\wedge dy_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dy_d,\\
 g=t-s+y^{\mathsf T}x,\\
 \eta_X=dt\wedge dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_d.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.1}
\]
The first kernel has output \(X\) and input \(Y\); the opposite
kernel has output \(Y\) and input \(X\). Both input top-form
lines are ungraded, with the displayed order. Their hypersurface
microlocal Hom classes use the positive relative connecting
representative and the shift \(\mathbb C_S[-1]\) of §5.61.

#### OI.0. Changing the pole order in the actual module

Write \(e_0\) for the forward class of \(\eta_Y/f\), and
\(\tau=D_t\). For every nonnegative integer \(r\), define
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 e_r=\frac{\tau^r}{r!}e_0,\\
 e_r=\left[\frac{\eta_Y}{f^{r+1}}\right].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.2}
\]
The second equality is an equality of actual relative classes.
Indeed \(D_t f=-1\), so induction differentiating the ordinary
holomorphic function on its sector complement gives
\(D_t^r(f^{-1})=r!f^{-r-1}\). The input frame is independent
of \(t\). The canonical action comparison FIM.5 and BI.1
identifies this finite differential action with the same action
in the shifted microlocal Hom.

The actual normal derivative is a two-sided unit in both
\(E_X\) and \(B_X\). Therefore
\[
 e_0=r!\tau^{-r}e_r.
 \tag{OI.3}
\]
This equality takes place in the module; it uses the proved
inverse in the operator ring. It makes no choice of a primitive
on the space of holomorphic functions. The map
\(P\mapsto Pe_r\) is consequently an isomorphism from the whole
output ring to the same incidence module, for either \(E\) or
\(B\): relative to the basis \(e_0\), it is right multiplication
of \(P\) by the unit \(\tau^r/r!\).

Let \(\mathcal L_0:B_Y\to B_X\) be the full input map of BI.25.
For every entire input symbol \(R\),
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 e_rR=\mathcal L_r(R)e_r,\\
 \mathcal L_r(R)=
 \tau^r\mathcal L_0(R)\tau^{-r}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.4}
\]
To prove the formula, move the input action past the output
operator \(\tau^r/r!\), use \(e_0R=\mathcal L_0(R)e_0\),
and insert the two adjacent inverse powers in OI.3.
The scalar \(r!\) cancels. All products are actual whole
products. LN.26–LN.28 identifies the displayed conjugation
with \(\mathcal H_r\mathcal L_0=\mathcal L_r\).
For an integer \(r\), that identification can also be read
directly from the finite Leibniz rule:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 (\tau^rP\tau^{-r})_j
 =\sum_{k=0}^r\binom rk\partial_t^k p_{j+k}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.5}
\]
There are finitely many terms for every input coefficient,
even when the positive head is infinite. The common-domain
product and Cauchy bounds of IK.2–IK.3 and BI.4 apply.
Thus OI.4 holds for the whole \(B\)-ring, rather than only
for polynomial input generators.

#### OI.1. The reverse class, phase and density

In output coordinates \((s,v)\) on \(Y\), the standard reversed
incidence has equation \(t-s-v^{\mathsf T}x=0\).
Its order-\(N\) pole class is OI.2 with \(r=d\).
Pull it back by the ordinary output coordinate reflection
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 F(s,y)=(s,-y),\quad v=-y,\\
 e^-=\left[\frac{\eta_X}{g^{d+1}}\right].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.6}
\]
This reflection acts on the output variables alone.
The relative input frame remains exactly \(\eta_X\).
There is no input Jacobian multiplier. Its complex output
Jacobian is \((-1)^d\), and its real Jacobian determinant
is \(|(-1)^d|^2=1\); the complex orientation is preserved.
The ordinary support and trace comparison of BCT.1–BCT.3
therefore transports the canonical class, with this same
ordered input frame.

Let \(J\) denote the whole output reflection on operators:
it fixes time and its derivative, and sends every spatial
coordinate and spatial derivative to its negative. OI.4
and the whole coordinate comparison give
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 e^-P=\Psi(P)e^-,\\
 \Psi=J\mathcal L_d=\mathcal L_0^{-1},\\
 \Psi:B_X\longrightarrow B_Y.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.7}
\]
Here the Legendre map before the reflection has input \(X\)
and output \((s,v)\); the final ring has the coordinates
\((s,y)\). The last equality is the entire inverse identity
LN.30. Its proof retains the complete negative tails and
the common positive-cutoff bounds. The equality is not
inferred merely from its generator values.

In particular its ordered time value is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Psi(t)=s+(E_y+d)\sigma^{-1},\\
 E_y=\sum_i y_iD_{y_i},\qquad \sigma=D_s.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.8}
\]
The shift by \(d\) is the pole-order normalization in OI.6.
Both \(e^-\) and the forward generator
\(e^+=[\eta_Y/f]\) belong to the injected whole-\(B\)
incidence modules of BI.A; each is a basis on both of its
operator sides. OI.3 proves that replacing the simple pole
by this higher pole does not lose any part of that module.

The reverse phase also gives exactly the inverse contact graph.
The output block of \(-\sigma\,dg\) is
\((\sigma,-\sigma x)\); its input block is
\((-\sigma,-\sigma y)\). After the required input antipodal
operation, the input \(X\) covector is \((\sigma,\sigma y)\).
Consequently, with \(z\) the input \(X\) projective covariable
and \(w\) the output \(Y\) projective covariable,
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 z=y,\quad w=-x,\quad g=0,\\
 (t,x,z)=\\
 (s+y^{\mathsf T}w,-w,y).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.9}
\]
This is the inverse in LI.9, including its time coordinate
and its antipodal signs.

#### OI.2. Both balanced bimodule evaluations

Set \(\phi=\mathcal L_0\), \(\psi=\phi^{-1}\).
Let \(H\) be the forward \((B_X,B_Y)\)-module with basis
\(e^+\), and \(K\) the opposite \((B_Y,B_X)\)-module with
basis \(e^-\). Their entire right actions are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 e^+Q=\phi(Q)e^+,\quad Q\in B_Y,\\
 e^-P=\psi(P)e^-,\quad P\in B_X.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.10}
\]
There are explicit bimodule isomorphisms
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{ev}_X:H\otimes_{B_Y}K
                 \longrightarrow B_X,\\
 Pe^+\otimes Qe^-\longmapsto P\phi(Q),
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.11}
\]
and
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{ev}_Y:K\otimes_{B_X}H
                 \longrightarrow B_Y,\\
 Qe^-\otimes Pe^+\longmapsto Q\psi(P).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.12}
\]
For OI.11 the balancing relation with \(R\in B_Y\)
has respective images \(P\phi(R)\phi(Q)\) and
\(P\phi(RQ)\), which are equal. Its right \(B_X\)-action
has image \(P\phi(Q\psi(A))=P\phi(Q)A\).
The left action is literal left multiplication.
Thus it is a bimodule map. Its inverse is
\[
 A\longmapsto Ae^+\otimes e^-.
 \tag{OI.13}
\]
Indeed the balancing relation moves \(Q\) in OI.11 to
the right action on \(e^+\); it then gives
\(Pe^+\otimes Qe^-=P\phi(Q)e^+\otimes e^-\).
This proves both inverse compositions on pure tensors,
which generate the algebraic tensor product.

For OI.12 the same verification is explicit:
the two balanced images are
\(Q\psi(A)\psi(P)\) and \(Q\psi(AP)\);
the right action by \(R\in B_Y\) has image
\(Q\psi(P\phi(R))=Q\psi(P)R\).
The inverse sends \(B\) to \(Be^-\otimes e^+\).
The two evaluation orders on a triple tensor agree:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 H\otimes_{B_Y}K\otimes_{B_X}H\longrightarrow H,\\
 Pe^+\otimes Qe^-\otimes P'e^+\\
 \longmapsto P\phi(Q)P'e^+,
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.14}
\]
and
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 K\otimes_{B_X}H\otimes_{B_Y}K\longrightarrow K,\\
 Qe^-\otimes Pe^+\otimes Q'e^-\\
 \longmapsto Q\psi(P)Q'e^-.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.15}
\]
For example the second association in OI.14 gives
\(Pe^+\bigl(Q\psi(P')\bigr)\), whose coefficient is
the displayed one by \(\phi\psi=1\). The second
association in OI.15 uses \(\psi\phi=1\).
These are the two triangle identities, with no scalar
left undetermined in the specified algebraic evaluations.

For every left \(B_X\)-module \(M\), the first evaluation
therefore induces
\[
 H\otimes_{B_Y}(K\otimes_{B_X}M)
                       \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }M.
 \tag{OI.16}
\]
On pure tensors the map is
\(Pe^+\otimes Qe^-\otimes m\mapsto P\phi(Q)m\);
its inverse sends \(m\) to \(e^+\otimes e^-\otimes m\).
OI.14 verifies the inverse using the balancing relations.
Interchanging \(X,Y\) gives the second natural inverse.
Both \(H\) and \(K\) are free of rank one on their right
sides, so the corresponding tensor functors preserve exact
sequences: identify them with a single copy of the module
as an abelian group, with action transported through the
ring isomorphism. The statement consequently applies
degree by degree to complexes and their cohomology.
It uses no extension flatness involving \(C\).

OI.11–OI.16 are algebraic tensor evaluations of the
specified actual bimodules. A holomorphic convolution
is instead a cup/excision/proper-trace map of relative
complexes. The identification of those analytic maps
with these evaluations requires its own argument.

#### OI.3. The two ordered normal residues

The forward-then-opposite pair, with endpoint input
\((t',x')\), has two normal factors
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f=s-t-x^{\mathsf T}y,\\
 g'=t'-s+y^{\mathsf T}x',\\
 A=t'-t+(x'-x)^{\mathsf T}y,\\
 g'=A-f.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.17}
\]
Fix \(A\ne0\), and choose \(0<r<|A|\).
The positively oriented \(s\)-circle is \(f=re^{i\theta}\);
here \(ds=df\) at fixed other variables. The ordered
normal period is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \frac1{2\pi i}\int_{|f|=r}
 \frac{df}{f(A-f)^N}\\
 =A^{-N}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.18}
\]
For a direct proof, the holomorphic function \((A-f)^{-N}\)
has a uniformly convergent Taylor expansion on this circle,
since it is holomorphic on a larger concentric disc of
radius less than \(|A|\). Termwise integration against
\(df/f\) leaves its constant term \(A^{-N}\).
The circle integral of every nonzero integer power is
zero by the parametrization \(f=re^{i\theta}\).

For the opposite-then-forward pair, with endpoint input
\((s',y')\), put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 g=t-s+y^{\mathsf T}x,\\
 f'=s'-t-x^{\mathsf T}y',\\
 A'=s'-s+(y-y')^{\mathsf T}x,\\
 f'=A'-g.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.19}
\]
Now \(dt=dg\), and the order-\(N\) pole comes first.
For \(0<r<|A'|\) the corresponding period is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \frac1{2\pi i}\int_{|g|=r}
 \frac{dg}{g^N(A'-g)}\\
 =(A')^{-N}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.20}
\]
Expand \((A'-g)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}g^k/(A')^{k+1}\)
uniformly on the circle. Only \(k=N-1\) survives.
Its coefficient is \((A')^{-N}\), with positive sign.
Thus reversing which factor has the higher pole gives
the same normal scalar; the intermediate normal
differential is first in both of the input frames OI.1.
These are ordinary holomorphic circle periods. The
degree-dependent signs of the derived proper trace
are additional data in an analytic convolution.

#### OI.4. Spatial boxes and every degenerate parameter

Let \(\epsilon_i>0\), and put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 Q=\prod_{i=1}^d[-\epsilon_i,\epsilon_i],\\
 V=\prod_{i=1}^d2\epsilon_i,\\
 B=\sum_i\epsilon_i|b_i|,\qquad |a|>B,\\
 F_d(a,b)=\\
 \int_Q
 \frac{dv_1\cdots dv_d}{(a+b^{\mathsf T}v)^{d+1}}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.21}
\]
An empty product is one and the \(d=0\) box is a point.
Both residues OI.18 and OI.20 give this spatial period,
with their respective endpoint differences substituted
for \(a,b\). On a compact parameter set inside \(|a|>B\),
choose one positive circle radius less than the minimum
of \(|a|-B\). Both iterated normal/spatial integrals are
then on a fixed compact circle times \(Q\), with a
strict common denominator bound. Ordinary Fubini follows
from uniform continuity and the finite Riemann sums on
these compact parameter rectangles. All fixed holomorphic
derivatives may be taken there by the Cauchy formula
on a slightly larger compact parameter set.

For \(b_i\ne0\) for every \(i\), put
\(a_\eta=a+\sum_i\eta_i\epsilon_i b_i\).
Then
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 F_d(a,b)=\frac{(-1)^d}{d!\prod_i b_i}\\
 {}\times\sum_{\eta\in\{-1,1\}^d}
       \frac{\prod_i\eta_i}{a_\eta}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.22}
\]
Indeed differentiation of the one denominator gives
\(\partial_a^d(a+b^{\mathsf T}v)^{-1}
=(-1)^d d!(a+b^{\mathsf T}v)^{-d-1}\).
On this function, \(\partial_a=b_i^{-1}\partial_{v_i}\).
Apply that equality in each spatial variable and integrate
the mixed derivative using the real fundamental theorem
of calculus. Upper faces give \(+\epsilon_i\), lower
faces give \(-\epsilon_i\), which gives exactly the
corner signs in OI.22. This is also LI.C with the
normal-pole factorial explicitly divided out.

Every apparent \(b_i=0\) singularity of OI.22 is removable
on the whole region \(|a|>B\). To prove the assertion,
on each compact with that strict bound expand the
integrand in its uniformly convergent geometric
derivative series. Termwise compact integration proves
holomorphy in every complex parameter, including zero
components of \(b\). This integral equals OI.22 on
the dense set with no zero component and hence is
its holomorphic extension. In particular
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 F_d(a,0)=Va^{-d-1},\\
 F_0(a)=a^{-1},\\
 F_1(a,b)=\frac{2\epsilon_1}
                  {a^2-\epsilon_1^2b^2}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.23}
\]
The first formula follows directly from the constant
integrand; the last follows by subtracting the two
corners in OI.22. The signs agree with both positive
normal residues.

There are fixed-domain bounds and explicit tails.
With \(q=B/|a|<1\), differentiating the geometric
series \(d\) times proves
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 (a+u)^{-d-1}=a^{-d-1}\\
 {}\times\sum_{m\ge0}\binom{d+m}{m}(-u/a)^m,\\
 |F_d(a,b)|\le\frac{V}{(|a|-B)^{d+1}}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.24}
\]
The summand after compact integration has norm at most
\(V|a|^{-d-1}\binom{d+m}{m}q^m\).
The sum of these positive bounds is the second line,
using \(\sum_m\binom{d+m}{m}q^m=(1-q)^{-d-1}\).
The latter identity is proved by differentiating the
geometric series inside its radius of convergence.
If \(q<q_1<1\), each term of that generating series
at \(q_1\) is at most its sum. Therefore the integrated
tail after degree \(R\ge0\) is at most
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 V|a|^{-d-1}(1-q_1)^{-d-1}\\
 {}\times\frac{(q/q_1)^{R+1}}{1-q/q_1}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{OI.25}
\]
All constants are fixed on a chosen compact with the
strict displayed margins. A further fixed Cauchy
margin gives the same normal convergence for every
specified parameter derivative. At \(b=0\), every
omitted term is zero directly.

#### The opposite module and the two types of evaluation

**Theorem OI.A.** The order-\(d+1\) opposite class OI.6
is a basis of the actual incidence module over each
whole operator side. Its entire right input map is
\(\mathcal L_0^{-1}\), in the ordered frame \(\eta_X\).
The forward and opposite modules have both balanced
evaluations OI.11–OI.12, with the two triangle identities,
and give inverse exact tensor functors on all modules.
The same statements hold for their finite-\(E\) restrictions.

**Proof.** OI.0 changes the pole order by an actual unit.
OI.1 gives its canonical reflected class, exact density,
inverse contact graph and full coefficient map.
OI.2 proves every balancing relation, the two inverse
evaluations and their triple identities explicitly.
All constructions commute with restriction, so the same
maps define the assertions for sheaves on their charts.
The ring maps restrict to the finite rings by LN.30.
\(\square\)

**Theorem OI.B.** On every compact subset of the strict
denominator region in OI.21, both ordered ordinary normal
residues are the same order-\(N\) denominator, and the
subsequent compact spatial periods are OI.21–OI.25.
The corner expressions extend over every vanishing
spatial parameter, including the fully degenerate point.

**Proof.** OI.3 evaluates both normal integrals, with
their respective first- and higher-order poles.
OI.4 gives common compact contours, the complete box
identities, all degeneracies and differentiated tails.
\(\square\)

The tensor evaluations and ordinary periods above do
not identify either normalized analytic kernel product.
That identification must retain every relative
complement entry, the actual intermediate-variable
proper collar, the all-degree trace signs and the
diagonal degree-\(N\) unit. In particular a positive
one-normal residue is not an equality with that
diagonal unit. No whole-real contact isomorphism or
arbitrary-holonomic regularization follows solely from
OI.A or OI.B.


Free primary context: [Benchoufi, *Action of micro-differential operators on quantized contact transformations*, arXiv:2102.08861v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.08861v2), Section 3. All arguments used above are proved here or in the exact earlier programme sections linked above.


## 6. What monodromy misses in the irregular world

Consider $\partial_t e=t^{-2}e$. A horizontal coefficient is $e^{1/t}$; its ordinary monodromy is trivial. The trivial connection also has trivial monodromy, but (1.5) proves these meromorphic connections are not isomorphic. For $t=r e^{i\theta}$,
\[
|e^{1/t}|=\exp(\cos\theta/r).                                  \tag{6.1}
\]
It decays in one half-plane and grows faster than every power in the other. The rays $\theta=\pm\pi/2$ separate those growth regimes. This rank-one example has no nontrivial Stokes gluing matrix: it displays the exponential rate that ordinary monodromy forgets.

For higher rank, formal exponential decompositions can be realized by different analytic gauges on different sectors. Their transition maps carry additional Stokes data. The irregular Riemann–Hilbert problem reconstructs the meromorphic connection from enhanced topological data that retain those asymptotic distinctions. This paragraph is a description of the problem, not a proof of a classification theorem.

Deligne, in letters to Malgrange of the late 1970s, organized boundary directions by the relative exponential growth rates and proposed the associated filtered local system. Sabbah's [*Introduction to Stokes structures*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.2762), Lectures 1–2, develops these Stokes-filtered local systems in dimension one.

Scholze's [*Wild Betti sheaves*, §1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24599), describes a universal enlargement of ordinary Betti sheaves with an exponential object and a Fourier equivalence. It recovers a construction of Tamarkin, also expressed through enhanced sheaves, and relates it to the irregular Riemann–Hilbert correspondence. The enlargement changes the coefficient category so that exponential information survives. We cite this construction as a modern framework; we do not identify ordinary finite-rank local systems with arbitrary irregular connections, or claim that this note alone proves the whole irregular correspondence.

## 7. Exercises with complete solutions

**Exercise 13.1 (easy).** Decide regularity at zero and infinity for $x\partial_x-\lambda$, $x^2\partial_x-1$, and $x^3\partial_x-x$.

**Solution.** On the punctured line their coefficients are respectively $\lambda/x$, $x^{-2}$ and $x^{-2}$. At zero the first has at most a simple pole, and the other two have double poles. They are respectively regular, irregular, irregular. Under (4.2) the coefficients are $-\lambda/y$, $-1$, $-1$, so all three are regular at infinity, with the last two nonsingular there. The last two define the same punctured connection; the statement does not identify their coherent extensions at zero.

**Exercise 13.2 (easy).** Show that $\mathcal O.e^x$ is irregular at infinity.

**Solution.** The formal symbol has $\partial_xe=e$. In the coordinate $y=x^{-1}$, $\partial_ye=-y^{-2}e$. Any rank-one lattice is $y^m\mathbb C[[y]]e$, with logarithmic coefficient $m-y^{-1}$. None is stable, so Theorem 1.1 proves irregularity. Analytically the horizontal coefficient $e^{-1/y}$ has exponential growth on sectors about the negative real $y$ axis, so Theorem 3.1 gives the same conclusion.

**Exercise 13.3 (medium).** Prove the second-order Fuchs criterion.

**Solution.** If $ta_1$ and $t^2a_2$ are holomorphic, (3.8) makes $\mathbb C\{t\}v+\mathbb C\{t\}\Theta v$ a stable lattice in the cyclic rank-two module. Conversely regularity makes the dual scalar solutions moderate. Their nonzero Wronskian $W$ is moderate and has scalar monodromy, so $W=t^\rho h$ with $h$ meromorphic. Its logarithmic derivative has at most a simple pole. Abel's identity $W'=-a_1W$ proves the first bound. A monodromy eigen-solution $w=t^\sigma g$, $g$ meromorphic and nonzero, has $w'/w$ of pole order at most one and $w''/w$ of order at most two. Dividing $Pw=0$ by $w$ gives (3.7), proving the second bound. Shrink the disc so the meromorphic unit factors have no zeros. For formal coefficients, use the continuation eigen-solutions and Laurent valuations constructed after (3.8); the same identities prove both bounds.

**Exercise 13.4 (medium).** Exhibit the isomorphism $E_\lambda\simeq E_{\lambda+1}$.

**Solution.** Define $e_\lambda\mapsto x^{-1}e_{\lambda+1}$. Indeed
\[
\partial_x(x^{-1}e_{\lambda+1})
=-x^{-2}e_{\lambda+1}+(\lambda+1)x^{-2}e_{\lambda+1}
=\lambda x^{-2}e_{\lambda+1}.
\]
Its inverse sends $e_{\lambda+1}$ to $x e_\lambda$. Both coefficients are units on $\mathbb G_m$. They need not be units on $\mathbb A^1$, so the formula alone does not identify extensions across zero.

**Exercise 13.5 (hard).** Classify regular singular connections on the punctured formal disc by pairs $(V,T)$ with $T\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$, up to conjugacy. Specify the field.

**Solution.** Work over $\mathbb C((t))$. A stable lattice exists by Theorem 1.1. Shift residue generalized eigenspaces by powers of $t$ until their eigenvalues lie in $\Sigma$; Lemma 2.1 proves stability and termination. Solve recurrence (2.2), whose operators are invertible, to remove all positive powers of $t$ from the matrix. Assign to the resulting constant model $(V,A)$ the automorphism $e^{-2\pi iA}$.

For any prescribed invertible $T$, its generalized eigenblocks and the finite nilpotent logarithm (2.6) construct a normalized $A$. Formula (2.5) proves that all morphisms between normalized constant models are constant intertwiners. Polynomial logarithms on the $T$-blocks prove that these are exactly the $T$-intertwiners. The constructions are therefore inverse equivalences, not merely a list of objects. Changing a basis conjugates $T$, and a conjugacy gives an isomorphism of connections. A formal connection over a general characteristic-zero field does not acquire a complex topological monodromy without additional choices or field extension; the stated classification uses the complex field.

## What this lesson does not prove

Theorem 5.27 constructs an actual coherent reflexive strict coefficient lattice for a finite meromorphic connection on a reduced analytic divisor, under the analytic transverse-disc hypotheses on every local divisor component. It proves normalization at all smooth points, strict membership, saturation and logarithmic stability at all singular points, and the support statement for coherent submodules and actual classes. Arbitrary subquotients are excluded by the explicit counterexample. The full characteristic cutoff, initial global analytic generator, half-order correspondence and arbitrary analytic proper-image theorem remain obligations in §5.27.12.

The theorems and propositions in §§5.19–5.26 prove the actual factorial-growth symbol construction, bounded division and units, finite stalk Noetherianity, exact faithful finite-module completion at the dummy zero section, fixed neighbourhood coherent kernels, the general bounded Rees ambient comparison, and actual descent for a supplied coherent generating lattice satisfying \(tL\subset hL\). The canonical strict cutoff across singular characteristic strata, the initial global analytic generator, any half-order theorem, and full analytic arbitrary proper/support-proper regularity remain separate obligations.

Theorem 3.3 proves Fuchs's criterion in every order for formal and convergent coefficients. Theorems 5.0 and 5.1 prove canonical logarithmic extensions, the full global algebraic connection/local-system correspondence, the algebraic curve and divisorial tests, and compactification independence. The proper compactification and GAGA inputs have exact earlier programme proofs; the coherent-extension, transverse-family, meromorphic-comparison and logarithmic-jet steps are proved here.

Theorem 5.2 proves the connection/regular-holonomic identification, including presentations on a dense open and the Serre closure of curve-regular connections. Theorem 5.3 proves analytic regularity of every normalized SNC meromorphic bundle with its exact good filtration and characteristic cycle. Theorem 5.4 proves the natural logarithmic and meromorphic de Rham comparisons by convergent Laurent homotopies, fine resolutions and exact cubical periods. Theorem 5.5 proves the full global algebraic de Rham comparison for every curve-regular algebraic connection, including nonproper and non-quasi-projective varieties, by the finite pole-layer and complex-linear GAGA arguments. Theorem 5.6 proves full generic Gauss–Manin regularity on every smooth algebraic base, with arbitrary curve base change, all coefficients and all fibre multiplicities in the curve lattice. Theorem 5.7 proves duality preservation for every regular holonomic module and bounded complex, with every support allowed. Theorem 5.8 proves relative analytic twist generation in every projective dimension for arbitrary coherent sheaves near a projective fibre; Lemma 5.8.2 also proves coherent higher images for projective-line projections. Theorem 5.9 and Lemma 5.9.1 prove locally projective coherent analytic images, with the initial coherent-generator hypothesis explicit for operator modules. Theorem 5.10 proves coherence, boundedness and analytic transported support of the cotangent candidate. Theorems 5.11–5.12 prove the singular-inclusive isotropic dimension bound and the actual output-filtration comparison, hence analytic projective holonomicity with the initial coherent-generator or global good-filtration hypothesis. Constructing that initial generator for every analytic regular holonomic module remains required. Theorem 5.13 proves the algebraic regular-holonomic SNC extension on every proper SNC pair and every open restriction, all boundary simple factors, and all algebraic curve pullbacks of these meromorphic modules. Theorems 5.14–5.17 prove full algebraic four-map regularity and the bounded-complex criterion using all smooth curve maps or only smooth locally closed curve immersions, including every singular support and every smooth separated finite-type ambient variety. Full analytic proper direct-image regularity remains required. Theorem 5.18 proves external-product and both tensor/dual tensor operations using the now-proved four-map and curve criterion. Full analytic proper regularity and the initial global analytic generator remain distinct obligations.

The Stokes description, the irregular Riemann–Hilbert problem and the wild Betti construction are cited perspectives. We prove no formal exponential decomposition, sectorial summation or irregular correspondence theorem. The earlier analytic flat-frame and Cauchy proofs are linked above. The product-growth estimate, removable-pole arguments and category gluing used here have explicit proofs in the lesson.
